Game Awards 2026: All Game of the Year Nominees and Predictions

📅 29 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1854 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that with less than a month to go until the 13th Game Awards, set for Dec.
  • At this point, we have a good idea of what games will be favored by The Game Awards' voting body: A high Metacritic rating (preferably over 90) is a must; role-playing games and action-adventures are strongly favored, as are games with strong narrative elements; indie and multiplayer games struggle harder for recognition than AAA single-player adventures.
  • Below, we pick the likely winner and rank the rest of the six nominees in order of their likeliness to win.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that with less than a month to go until the 13th Game Awards, set for Dec. 10, every key competitor has finally shown its hand, and the best (or biggest, at any rate) was saved for last. Now that's out of the way, and nominations have been declared, we have a clear picture: As in 2025, there is an extremely clear favorite that seems all but impossible to unseat.

At this point, we have a good idea of what games will be favored by The Game Awards' voting body: A high Metacritic rating (preferably over 90) is a must; role-playing games and action-adventures are strongly favored, as are games with strong narrative elements; indie and multiplayer games struggle harder for recognition than AAA single-player adventures. We used these metrics to correctly predict last year's winner, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, and the 2024 winner, Astro Bot. In 2025, we also predicted all six GOTY nominees and correctly called 20 other categories.

Below, we pick the likely winner and rank the rest of the six nominees in order of their likeliness to win. We'll find out whether there will be a shock upset at The Game Awards on Dec. 10.

Upgrade (Nov. 25): This week, we begin making predictions for what will win every major category at The Game Awards 2026; you'll find them below our ranking of the six Game of the Year contenders. This first update contains predictions for the indie, multiplayer, and mobile categories, plus a few odds and ends. Next week, we'll predict the genre cateogory winners, and in the week of the awards themselves will predict the craft awards .

Why it could win: The biggest game production in history with the highest Metacritic score of all time, GTA 6 compromises on absolutely nothing, from technically astonishing visuals to deep gameplay systems and nuanced storytelling. The added X factor is Rockstar's infallible sense of cool. It's nominated in every category it's reasonably eligible for. Nothing else this year is even close to its league.

Recent findings suggest that weaknesses: Basically none, aside from the narrative that its win is inevitable, which might spur some voters to make another pick. Rockstar has been beaten before, notably by God of War when Red Dead Redemption 2 competed at the 2018 Game Awards, but there is no competition that strong this year.

Recent findings suggest that momentum (holding steady): GTA 6 has a Metascore of 99, the highest in the history of the awards. The prediction markets put its chances of victory at 96%. It's even more locked in than Clair Obscur was last year. There is no way it isn't winning.

Industry observers note that why it could win: Resident Evil is a reliable contender at The Game Awards, with three GOTY nominations since 2019, and many more in other categories. Requiem combines the fan appeal of the remakes with the freshness of a upcoming entry, and blends their gameplay successfully, too. It's slickly produced, digestible, thrilling, with both global appeal and a serious side: a perfect Game Awards GOTY contender.

Weaknesses: Requiem's critical reception was very good overall, but perhaps a tiny bit soft to be a true GOTY contender — it sits in the high 80s on Metacritic and OpenCritic. Released in February, so recency bias is not on its side and it may not feel so exciting to voters as some more recent games.

In a recent development, momentum (holding steady): Everything below GTA 6 is a rounding error, but the prediction markets narrowly favor Ocarina of Time over Requiem for second place. That's wrong — a remake would never be bestowed with the Game of the Year title. Requiem is tied for second on nominations and remains a down-the-middle Game Awards favorite that has been in the runner-up spot all year. That hasn't changed.

Read Giovanni Colantonio's full review of Resident Evil Requiem.

Recent findings suggest that why it could win: Developer Remedy gets to have its cake and eat it at The Game Awards: It's a purveyor of mainstream, cinematic action-adventures that retains a level of indie authenticity and cool. It's usually rewarded with plenty of nominations, and both the first Control and Alan Wake 2 were GOTY nominees. Control Resonant hasn't broken the streak.

Weaknesses: A genre switch from tight shooter to open-world action-RPG has met with a pretty mixed response, and although Resonant's Metacritic rating is actually higher than the original Control's (83 to 82), the sentiment seems decidedly cooler — perhaps because, as a sequel, it has lost the element of surprise.

Sources indicate that momentum (📈 from No. 6): Control Resonant defied its mixed reception with a very strong six nominations, tied with Resident Evil: Requiem. It's nominated in the key categories of Game Direction and Narrative. It's perhaps the likeliest candidate to take a win off GTA 6, in the Art Direction category. In anything other than a GTA year, it would be a classic dark horse.

Read Willa Rowe's full review of Control Resonant.

In a recent development, why it could win: Phantom Blade Zero is this year's Black Myth: Wukong, a visually spectacular action game from an exciting upcoming Chinese studio that muscled its way into the GOTY race. Unlike Black Myth, and unlike this year's Korean competitor Crimson Desert, it's got strong reviews (88 on Metacritic, 90 on OpenCritic).

Weaknesses: While it has reviewed well, Phantom Blade hasn't quite pulled away from a crowded action-adventure field that includes Control Resonant and 007 First Light.

Momentum (holding steady): Phantom Blade Zero has done very well to secure five nominations, including the crucial Game Direction nod. International jurors who don't fancy voting for the Western hegemony of GTA 6 might well pick it.

Read Paulo Kawanishi's full review of Phantom Blade Zero.

According to recent reports, why it could win: A beloved classic, with a reputation as the best game ever made, lavishly remade by a team at the top of their game, and showered in critical plaudits like no other game this year aside from GTA 6. It may be just a remake, but Nintendo has mustered a huge sense of event around Ocarina, from its dramatic visual reinvention to its bold positioning against GTA 6 in the calendar. It also benefits from its aesthetic contrast with the front-runner: a cozy, fantastical family adventure.

Weaknesses: After all, though, it's still a remake of an old game, and a very faithful one. The jury has recognized Nintendo's achievement here (as it did for the likes of Resident Evil 4 and Final Fantasy 7 Remake in the past), but a Game of the Year win seems inconceivable for such a well-known quantity.

Momentum (📉 from No. 3): With its 96 Metascore and beloved reputation, Ocarina is the most likely GTA spoiler on paper. But nominating a game is different from selecting it to win, and I think any remake would struggle to overcome that hurdle. Its lack of nominations in Game Direction and Narrative show its weakness in the eyes of the jury: In 2026, as a remake, it's a technical achievement only.

Read Giovanni Colantonio's full review of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

According to recent reports, why it could win: IO Interactive's debut James Bond game has made a confident splash with critics, earning a decent 87 Metascore. This kind of slick, cinematic action-adventure usually goes down well with the jury, while the inclusion of some of Hitman developer IO's trademark "social stealth" gameplay lends it additional gamer cred.

Weaknesses: No licensed game has ever won Game of the Year (unless you count Baldur's Gate 3 and The Witcher 3), and First Light's critical reception is a little soft, with some reviewers unimpressed by IO's shift in a more commercial direction.

Momentum (re-entry): No game has ever missed a nomination for Best Game Direction and gone on to win Game of the Year. That would disqualify First Light even in a competitive year, and this isn't a competitive year.

Read Ford James' full review of 007 First Light.

It has been revealed that as is often the case, Best Indie is one of the most exciting and hotly contested awards of the night, with an extremely strong field. Any of them would be a deserving winner, and this year there hasn't been a breakout hit that will pull away on grounds of sheer popularity. Massive Walk is the most innovative and eye-catching game here, though, and through its modestly viral multiplayer nature, has got the closest to breaking containment.

In a recent development, the three most visible games in this category, and likeliest to harvest votes from The Game Awards' broad, normie-leaning jury, are Dressmaker, Esoteric Ebb, and Orbitals. Were it not for the inherent gender bias in the games media that makes up the jury, it should be an easy win for Dressmaker, but in this sad reality, I suspect it's between the funny, nerdy RPG Esoteric Ebb and the cool and approachable co-op game Orbitals. The jury has form with favoring co-op adventures, so Orbitals it is.

In a recent development, this inexplicable category has even more inexplicable nominees than usual in 2026. Has the jury forgotten that Life is Strange: Reunion is not good? What is the "pro-social meaning or message" of Big Walk? House House's multiplayer game is the big beast in the category, but I think the jury will be inclined to go with something more character-driven and narrative-focused, so I'm going for the next-most-famous game here, Mixtape.

In a recent development, while the jury is happy to pick shooters to win this award, it usually avoids big, established names like Call of Duty and Gears of War, and often seems to prefer co-op to competitive games. Meccha Chameleon is a sensation, but too scrappy and unpolished for the jury's tastes, while Big Walk has the glow of prestige and critical acclaim.

Sources indicate that the Game Awards jury has form for congratulating CD Projekt for updating its single-player RPGs in this category: Cyberpunk 2077 won in 2023. There's no redemption narrative in the case of The Witcher 3 as there is with Cyberpunk or No Man's Sky, but I've a feeling the warm familiarity most feel for this former GOTY winner, and the decent reception for its upcoming, free remaster, will work in its favor.

It's a familiar complaint, but the jury seems to have a very narrow understanding of mobile gaming that boils down to gacha RPGs and brand extensions for console franchises. Fortunately, there's a game this year that both fits the profile and is legitimately good, so Arknights: Endfield is going to take it.

The only credible competition for Zach Cregger's barnstorming Resident Evil movie is the second season of the Fallout show, which is a previous winner. This is an automatic win.

This category is something of a stacked deck; four 2027 games up against a more distant prospect that's a measurably bigger deal in every sense. It looks like CD Projekt is going home with two Game Awards this year.

Why Quentin Tarantino Didn't Direct Brad Pitt's Cliff Booth Movie

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (885 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Warning: This article contains spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.".
  • If it looks like a Quentin Tarantino movie and talks like a Quentin Tarantino movie, you'd usually find yourself watching a Quentin Tarantino movie.
  • In a recent development, after having finally seen the highly-anticipated sequel for ourselves, we (and many others) were left with even more questions regarding why Tarantino ultimately decided to sit this one out rather than sit in the director's chair himself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Warning: This article contains spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.".

If it looks like a Quentin Tarantino movie and talks like a Quentin Tarantino movie, you'd usually find yourself watching a Quentin Tarantino movie. "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is the rare exception to that rule, however. After "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" debuted in 2019 and was heralded by many as the filmmaker's best movie yet, whispers of a continuation soon grew to a deafening noise. Tarantino then went and wrote a book based on the events of the film in a sort of reverse-adaptation situation. He subsequently spent months talking up his intentions to direct a since-shelved project called "The Movie Critic," which would've starred Brad Pitt reprising his role as Cliff Booth. But after that fell apart, David Fincher eventually came on board to direct Tarantino's script for "Cliff Booth.".

In a recent development, after having finally seen the highly-anticipated sequel for ourselves, we (and many others) were left with even more questions regarding why Tarantino ultimately decided to sit this one out rather than sit in the director's chair himself. "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is a solid enough spiritual successor, albeit one where Fincher and Tarantino's unique (and wildly different) sensibilities seem to clash more often than complement. And the snappiness of the dialogue, tone, and rhythm and pacing certainly feel indebted to the quintessential Tarantino style most of us know and adore.

In a recent development, so, with all due respect to a legend like Fincher, was there ever a world where Tarantino had simply directed this himself? It's a complicated question with no easy answers, but below, we've rounded up a complete timeline of events — to the best of public knowledge, of course. So, here's why Tarantino's "Cliff Booth" instead became a Fincher/Tarantino joint.

It all began, as it so often does in this business, with a project that wasn't to be. In 2023, "The Movie Critic" was breathlessly announced as Quentin Tarantino's 10th and final directing gig — a self-imposed limit that the ever-opinionated artist decided to stick to, no matter what. And while rumors initially suggested this might have been based on the life of prolific writer and critic Pauline Kael, it was later revealed that this would've been an original story taking QT's usual fast-and-loose approach to fact and fiction. All seemed ready and raring to go ... until Tarantino appeared to rethink his approach (following rewrites that delayed production) and dropped the project altogether.

In a recent development, but Hollywood just loves a comeback story, and this wasn't the end of the line. In 2025, news broke that Fincher would be directing a sequel to "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" focused on stuntman extraordinaire Cliff Booth. It didn't take much brain power to connect the dots between the two film ideas, leading to much informed speculation that Tarantino reworked his idea for "The Movie Critic" into what turned out to be "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth." For his part, Tarantino spoke to The Hollywood Reporter in 2025 and denied that Cliff was ever going to appear in "The Movie Critic." Of course, this contradicts other accounts claiming that a sort of cinematic universe may have been in the works. We'll likely never know the full behind-the-scenes story.

Sources indicate that did we receive the next-best outcome in its place? A Fincher/QT dream team has been years in the making, after all. Still, we can't help but wonder about what might have been.

For better or worse, what's clear is that "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" seems fated to divide viewers. There are those who feel David Fincher's involvement as director meshes beautifully with Quentin Tarantino's skills as writer, leading to a final result that's even more than the sum of its mighty parts — akin to what Fincher pulled off in his collaboration with Aaron Sorkin on "The Social Network," for instance. But there are others who feel that, while the tension between their particular styles and worldviews makes for dramatically interesting material, the push and pull between Fincher and Tarantino ultimately proves too unwieldy.

Industry observers note that yes, I happen to fall into that latter camp (if you haven't guessed as much already), and it's tough to reconcile the movie we have with the hypothetical version it could've been. To be fair, the evidence is fairly plain to see. Where "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" is overflowing with warmth and nostalgia and a poignant perspective of time passing us by (and, okay, a whole lot of gratuitous violence, too), "Cliff Booth" stands out for how emotionally distant and cold it feels in practically every scene ... outside of Cliff's flirtations with Elizabeth Debicki's Karen Crosby or bonding moments with father Gus (Peter Weller), at least.

In the hands of Tarantino alone, it's fair to wonder if he could've brought a much-needed sense of fun and verve to the action that seems oddly missing in "Cliff Booth." What we ended up with is something caught between a Fincher and Tarantino film. Instead of half of both, wouldn't it have been more satisfying to get all of Tarantino?

"The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" is now playing in select theaters.

Latest Update: TV Took the Wrong Lessons from the Success of ‘Heated Rivalry’

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that many have classified the success of “Heated Rivalry” as an enigma, a phenomenon that burst out of Crave original containment and superseded even the most optimistic expectations.
  • There is a great deal of “right place, right time” to the success of the show, but is it possible “Heated Rivalry” wasn’t just the stars aligning, but a well-timed adaptation with all the right components that met an audience ready to buy in?
  • Based on the second book in Rachel Reid’s series “Game Changers,” “Heated Rivalry” follows competitive ice hockey rivals, curly-haired Russian Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie) and freckled Canadian Shane Hollander (Hudson Williams).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that many have classified the success of “Heated Rivalry” as an enigma, a phenomenon that burst out of Crave original containment and superseded even the most optimistic expectations. In early 2026, episodes averaged more than 10.6 million viewers in the U.S. alone. The show became the most-watched scripted title acquired in HBO Max history and Bell Media’s most successful original streaming series.

There is a great deal of “right place, right time” to the success of the show, but is it possible “Heated Rivalry” wasn’t just the stars aligning, but a well-timed adaptation with all the right components that met an audience ready to buy in? With all its success, you’d think there are plenty of lessons to be learned from the show, but are the studios even listening? Related Stories Oobah Butler Wants to Expose the World’s Stupidest Industries, but They Get Worse Faster Than He Can Initiative His Stunts Fixing Netflix’s TV Problem: 5 Changes the Streamer Should Make for Better, Sturdier, and Buzzier Series.

Based on the second book in Rachel Reid’s series “Game Changers,” “Heated Rivalry” follows competitive ice hockey rivals, curly-haired Russian Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie) and freckled Canadian Shane Hollander (Hudson Williams). Over six episodes spanning nearly a decade, the show follows the pair’s complex relationship as they compete as league rivals while beginning an adrenaline-pumping affair that proves more compelling than Stanley Cup wins.

The show premiered in November 2025 to a modest audience, predominantly Reid’s readers, before word-of-mouth promotion boosted Jacob Tierney’s show onto a global stage.

First and foremost, “Heated Rivalry” clearly indicates an appetite for LGBTQ+ stories. The series has been celebrated for its unabashed portrayal of queer desire between two men in an environment of deeply ingrained homophobia and rigid expectations of masculinity.

While Storrie and Williams may beautifully perform “Heated Rivalry”’s depiction of queerness, the show’s heart is Tierney, a gay creator, writer, director, and executive producer whose brushstrokes eloquently articulate the fear, excitement, and intimacy of burgeoning queer infatuation. Tierney’s show is the product of a creator fulfilling their vision, uninterrupted by studio censorship or executive meddling.

Ultimately, the content of “Heated Rivalry” isn’t revolutionary, but its far-reaching viewership is: it reveals the profound longing for queer storytelling in the romance genre.

It’s telling then that, in the wake of “Heated Rivalry,” a wave of upcoming shows have latched onto hockey rather than LGBTQ+ characters. Since “Heated Rivalry” premiered one year ago, Prime Video’s adaptation of Elle Kennedy’s college hockey romance series “Off Campus” aired its first season and was renewed for a second season before the series premiere, while Netflix greenlit an adaptation of Hannah Grace’s “Icebreaker” novels. (The streamer is also releasing the YA hockey drama “The Sticks.”).

This doesn’t speak to the merit of each production, which arrive with their own fanbases and selling points, but to a wider complaint about how to capitalize on a moment. But there is no doubt that the ramped-up attention on these hockey shows is beholden to the success of “Heated Rivalry.” Yet, what has carried over is the game on the ice, not the potential of queer romance — especially eyebrow-raising when GLAAD reported LGBTQ+ characters on TV have dropped 25 percent over the past year.

Furthermore, it’s not just the TV industry that has failed to recognize this moment truly; even the National Hockey League has shown very little love for the hit show, despite “Heated Rivalry” undoubtedly contributing toward the 1.8 million viewers who tuned in to ice hockey for the first time last season, as ESPN reported of the National Hockey League’s research.

Another facet of the show’s success is casting unknowns, something the James Bond team continue to veto. Arriving on screen unburdened by the baggage of previous recognizable roles, Storrie and Williams were blank canvases on which to paint their characters and their burgeoning fling-turned-romance. There’s a sense of exciting discovery, with audiences investing in a character while uncovering a newcomer’s talent. For instance, many said they believed Storrie was a Russian man until the charming press tour revealed he grew up in Texas.

Sources indicate that it is apparent that bringing new faces into the fold is deemed unfavourable, with no established star power to lure in fans. Despite this concern, casting discussions also face pushback, as we repeatedly see the same batch of actors time and time again, to the point that their roles start to blend. With its casting decisions, “Heated Rivalry” launched the careers of its central duo, Storrie and Williams, swiftly becoming two of the most exciting rising stars of the moment.

It has been revealed that the pair are a prime example of the stardom potential that comes with investing in and trusting talent. The fine acting chops of Storrie and Williams are certainly part of the reason “Heated Rivalry” has been successful; while they discovered Ilya and Shane, viewers also discovered Connor and Hudson, a journey that wouldn’t be as impactful if they had notable pre-existing credits.

According to recent reports, “Heated Rivalry” also appears in a highly populated sea of book-to-screen romance projects, a competitive arena where adaptations can split viewers for disloyalty to the source material. “Heated Rivalry” hit a sweet spot.

Sources indicate that tierney is true to the essence of Reid’s book, not trying to outrun the words on the page. Additionally, Tierney doesn’t shy away from the romance genre, and you don’t need to understand the rules of hockey to latch onto the amorous bond of the two hockey captains. The show’s success in this regard could be viewed as a template (fans of the book love it for a reason, an overhaul is widely unnecessary). Yet a string of recent popular book adaptations has been criticised for turning their backs on the books, from watering down sex scenes in “People We Meet on Vacation” to major plot alterations in “Every Year After”.

Though “Heated Rivalry” has left its mark — celebrated for LGBTQ+ representation, casting unknowns and its elevated adaptation — has the show changed anything?

Taking a risk on bold strokes seems worth it when a show from a Canadian streamer goes on to make over $1.4 million from a limited theatrical release across 945 movie theaters in early November screenings. The show’s cultural relevance and staying power are a breakthrough, but a year after its premiere, it seems very little has been learned so far.

'Wifi Motion Sensing' Can Track Everything You Do Through Your Router

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A simple wifi feature could let ISPs track your location and movement patterns within your home.
  • While the technology isn’t universally implemented just yet and is typically opt-in only (smart home consumers might want the movement tracking feature for lights and heating), it presents quite a few privacy risks.
  • Wifi routers rely on radio signals to connect wirelessly to your devices and appliances.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A simple wifi feature could let ISPs track your location and movement patterns within your home. "Wifi motion sensing" turns your ISP’s router into a motion detector, letting providers know exactly how many people are in the house, where they are situated, individual movement patterns, and, in some cases, even body shapes that could approximate a person’s identity.

While the technology isn’t universally implemented just yet and is typically opt-in only (smart home consumers might want the movement tracking feature for lights and heating), it presents quite a few privacy risks. So here’s how wifi routers sense motion, what they can do with it, who has access to the data, and how you can disable it.

Wifi routers rely on radio signals to connect wirelessly to your devices and appliances. Those same radio signals are also absorbed and reflected by the human body as they travel in all directions from the router. With the right software, ISPs can track how those wifi signals travel around your room, which can be studied to detect presence and sense motion patterns.

As long as your ISP’s router model supports this feature natively, it doesn’t require any additional hardware to be installed in your home. For example, Xfinity’s version of the feature pairs your router with five other connected appliances in your room to create oval-shaped sensing zones that can track your presence and movement within those spaces.

Sources indicate that it isn’t a new feature, either—companies like Cognitive Systems and Origin Wireless that supply networking hardware to ISPs have been offering wifi motion sensing for years now, while early research prototypes from the MIT date back at least as far as 2015. In 2025, IEEE updated its Wi-Fi 802.11 standard to include motion sensing and lay out the architectural guidelines for it, which makes it likely that even more routers will now ship with the feature.

In its current consumer form, wifi motion sensing can help you control smart home apparatus like lights or thermostats, get pet safety notifications on your phone, set up a fall alert system for elderly owners, and trigger appliances remotely based on human presence. But enabling it carries risks.

Recent findings suggest that most providers, including Cognitive Systems, claim that the technology isn’t sensitive to identity and can’t be used to track specific individuals. But even if true, that’s more likely to be a product decision rather than a technical limitation. Karlsruhe Institute researchers have shown that even ordinary wifi signals can identify individuals with a 99.5% accuracy.

Also worth noting: ISPs’ legal wording suggests that they may disclose the collected and stored motion data at any time to law enforcement, government agencies, regulators, and courts in response to subpoenas or during an emergency. ISPs may also retain your motion data in the cloud long-term in case they are required to facilitate a subpoena in the future.

According to recent reports, as far as major ISPs are concerned, Xfinity (Comcast) is the only broadband provider that presently offers this feature across its commercial routers on the XB7, XB8, XB9, XB10, MXB1, and XER10 gateways. It’s opted out by default, but in case you or a family member already switched it on, you can disable it again by navigating to Home > WiFi Motion on the Xfinity app, click on the gear icon on the live view page, and tap Remove WiFi Motion.

Industry observers note that verizon Fios customers also had access to a Home Awareness feature on their routers that could be toggled on or off using the MyFios app, but that’s since been discontinued. In an official disclosure published shortly after the discontinuation, Verizon notified customers that it has deleted all associated movement logs from this service and no longer retains any motion data from people.

Industry observers note that but there are other regional ISPs that offer it, too. For example, Breezeline (Atlantic Broadband) offers a feature called Motion within its Plume-powered application that alerts customers when movement is detected in their homes, among its other features. MidCo, a telecom organization in the Upper Midwest, has a feature called Sense which can be toggled on or off using the MidCo Wi-Fi app. Plume, ADT-owned Origin Wireless, and Airties—all of whom supply technology to ISPs—have also been marketing motion sensing to customers for the last few years.

If you’re unsure if your wifi router or ISP has motion sensing features or opts you in by default, look for a feature called “Sense,” “Motion,” or equivalent in your broadband’s mobile app. Exact steps differ greatly from one ISP to another, so it’s best not to assume that they will all opt you out by default, or that they collect the same types of data. With the 802.11bf upgrade to IEEE standards in 2025, this technology will be accessible to even more router manufacturers, so expect adoption to grow among internet providers as well.

In a recent development, like its predecessor, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is packed with talent, on and off-camera. With Quentin Tarantino penning the Once Upon a Time… in Hollywood sequel, but handing the directing reins over to David Fincher, there’s no doubt Brad Pitt’s return as the former eponymous stuntman is guaranteed to wow audiences when it hits theaters and IMAX before heading to Netflix next month.

In the movie, it’s been eight years since Booth went toe to toe with the Manson family. Now, he’s working as a bartender and a theater projectionist, but still putting his exceptional skills to work as a fixer for Hollywood’s elite. When he gets a call from Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), the talent agent of TV superstar Charlie Peters (Scott Caan), Booth is curious why a man known to perform his own stunts would need his aid. His instincts are spot-on, and Booth finds himself tangled up in a whole fresh mess, with a whole host of characters, played by Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Timothy Olyphant, and more.

In this interview with Steve Weintraub, Debicki and Caan open up about their nerves leading up to production with filmmaking titans like Fincher and Tarantino. They also discuss Fincher’s genius direction, his precision over things like Caan’s montage, and Debicki shares what it was like filming the balcony scene where Karen slaps Cliff Booth. Don’t miss the full conversation in the video above, with a transcript provided below.

COLLIDER: You've both been in a number of projects, but I am curious, as an actor, when you land the Fincher role, and it's written by Q.T., how much are you in your head a little bit more in the days leading up to that first day of filming, thinking about everything and how you want to play the role, and the preparation that goes into it?

In a recent development, ELIZABETH DEBICKI: You know what? It's funny, I didn't think about this, obviously, while it was happening, but in retrospect, the really interesting thing about working with David is he is so wildly intelligent as a filmmaker and a human being that you don't think that much, and that's kind of his gift to you as an actor.

You have this impeccable script. It is a gift to you that you will soon get to dip into and figure out how to do it with these amazing actors, and then you have David, who already knows what he wants. He knows how he's going to get you there. And so actually, it's super freeing.

Recent findings suggest that my memories of gearing up to do this, it's like, yes, we would be a little nervous every now and then if we had, like, a big monologue that day. But once you get one or two out of the way, it's like, then you're just having a good time. So, it's kind of a uniquely fun set, I think.

Industry observers note that SCOTT CAAN: I agree. Once we're doing it, all that stuff went away. But certainly, it's not about the result. It's about, “I want to make them happy that they made the decision to cast me in this part,” you know? So, I definitely was nervous.

Industry observers note that but I also think as actors, you know, I have a friend of mine who’s a fighter, and he noted, “The one time I lost a fight and got beaten up really badly was when I wasn't nervous.” So I think it's good for us to have those feelings. I think if you go into something like, “I got this,” you're going to get knocked out. So, I definitely had those feelings, but I embrace those feelings, and I think that's part of what we do. And I think it's notable to own your nervousness — and I definitely was… I don't think nervous is the right word, but anxious and wanted to do good, and wanted to make sure that they don't say, “We hired the wrong person.”.

DEBICKI: Scott, they would never say that a million years.

One of the things that really makes the audience erupt is you getting to slap Brad Pitt, and I think one of the reasons it's so effective is the way David directs the scene. It's not just you outside of the balcony. There's a camera shot from inside, where Brad hits the glass. Can you talk about filming that? Scott, I loved the movie montage, if you will, about your career, and the way that you're in these different projects. Talk a little bit about filming that and giving all that backstory because it's all so effective.

Industry observers note that DEBICKI: Well, the balcony scene is an extraordinary piece of writing. I think it's like an eight or 10-page scene, and it was always like this meal that we knew we were going to get to eat, like we were going to get there one day and shoot that scene. And it's unlike anything I've ever read or played, actually. The dynamic of these two people is so unique.

That second slap, I might be wrong, but my memory of this is we were set up inside shooting the scene that precedes it, and so we were already inside the apartment shooting the scene with Gus sleeping, when we wake him up, and I think that David being David and Erik [Messerschmidt] being Erik just sort of looked at it and went, “Oh, we’ve got to shoot it from inside because that's the cut that you want.” And so we did it.

According to recent reports, I think we shot that first, and then we went outside the next day and started the scene. Something like that. But it's just genius. It's genius cinematography, and Brad [Pitt] is an incredible stuntman. He really is.

CAAN: I think with those things, and David, I've never worked with somebody that has ideas that are so specific. There are a couple of times in the movie I was doing a scene, and he would say, “This is my idea…” and I’d go, “Alright, I'm going to do it. I don't quite…” And then I see the movie, and I go, “Oh, now I see.” I've never worked for someone who has that many great ideas that when you see the movie, you go, “Oh, I see that one, I see that one, I see that one.”.

It has been revealed that specifically, to answer your question about the documentary, the way that was done, as an actor, I just did what he told me to do. He was like, “Okay, for this, I'm going to need you to do this, and for this, I'm gonna need you to do this.” Like the scene with Timothy [Olyphant], obviously, and the scene in the parlor, those were acted scenes, but everything else was just in his brain. He and Quentin figured out what they wanted to do, and it was like, “Alright, hold the tennis racket. Flip your cigarette.” That was just me following what David wanted me to do.

Sources indicate that DEBICKI: That scene with Timothy and you was so good. It's really one of my favorite parts of the film.

Industry observers note that CAAN: I love that. That was fun. Timothy’s so good.

DEBICKI: It's so good. It's so funny and brilliant.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When it comes to making a movie sequel like "Focker In-Law," the challenges faced by the returning cast and crew are distinct but dependent on those faced by the newcomers. The former have to try not to repeat themselves, while the latter have to find a way of integrating their work into an already-established milieu. This can be especially tricky when it comes to comedy, as the genre lives and dies on tone and timing. If one or both are off, it can destroy the entire proceedings.

Recent findings suggest that these are the precise challenges that writer/director John Hamburg and star Ariana Grande had to deal with while making "Focker In-Law," the fourth film in the uber-popular "Meet the Parents" franchise. While returning folks like Ben Stiller (as Greg Focker) and Robert De Niro (as Jack Byrnes) could rely on their past work on the property to use as a starting point, Grande had to find a path to her own comedic voice within the film's ensemble. Not making it any easier is the fact that her role is not only key, but complex: She's Olivia Jones, the bride-to-be of Greg's son, Henry (Skyler Gisondo), yet Greg is trepidatious of anyone marrying his boy. Making things more complicated is that Olivia and Greg start off on a bad note that only gets worse, as Greg discovers her past as a former FBI hostage negotiator. This means Grande has to be both a sweet-natured love interest and a potentially conniving antagonist, which is not an easy mix.

When I had the chance to talk with Hamburg about this, he agreed that the challenge was not insignificant. Yet he also revealed how he worked with Grande to craft her character, especially in the editing room, resulting in a great upcoming addition to the Focker saga.

Recent findings suggest that as John Hamburg told me during our chat, it was not lost on himself and the others behind "Focker In-Law" that Ariana Grande had her work cut out for her playing Olivia. Yet, he explained why Grande was so uniquely qualified to handle the challenge:.

"We were like, 'Oh my God, she's playing the love interest and the antagonist. What a tight rope.' But honestly, she's so uniquely gifted that I think she's the only person that could really nail that thing where you're kind of scared of her, you're intimidated, but she's also the sweetest, most loving [person]. Her smile lights up a room. Ari brings so much of that energy, but she's just a wonderful actress. So, she could play all those levels.".

Recent findings suggest that it turns out that Grande's ability to play multiple levels of a character dovetailed nicely with Hamburg's approach to comedy, which is less about improvisation and more about tweaking the tone and intention of a moment or scene. Hamburg explained how Grande provided him with ample material that he was able to use in post-production:.

"[...] When we're filming, I try to get different levels. 'So, okay, maybe try it a little more passive-aggressive, or try it a little more hostile, or say this with a smile,' that kind of thing. And she has so much in her toolbox that she was able to give me so many levels. So, when I got to the editing room, it was like an embarrassment of riches to try while I was crafting her performance.".

The wrong person playing Olivia could've sunk the whole film. Fortunately, Hamburg had the right instinct that Grande could handle it.

"Focker In-Law" is at the moment playing in theaters.

The ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case with Flex Stand is perfect for those who want a more premium look for their iPhone Duo. If you’ve ever used a light-colored leather case before, you know it usually shows every stain and smudge it comes across, but ESR built the Atelier to resist daily wear and wipe clean.

Both cases share ESR’s Flex Stand, and it’s one of the most innovative and versatile parts of the lineup. It’s a 180-degree rotating stand made from zinc alloy, so it holds its shape even after months of propping up your iPhone. A precision hinge with damping control lets it open smoothly and lock at the angle you choose, whether the iPhone Duo is folded or unfolded, and ESR notes it has passed 3,000 open-and-close tests. In real life, that means propping the iPhone Duo open on a desk for a video call or on an airplane tray table for a movie, then using the stand as a grip when you’re holding it.

Both cases add extra hinge protection and raised edges where a foldable is most exposed. If you follow our MagSafe Monday column, you know magnetic strength really matters for MagSafe wallets, car mounts, etc. The Classic Hybrid has 1,500g of magnetic hold, and the Atelier has 1,400g.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case for iPhone Duo is 15% off.

The same two incredible cases come in iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max versions, and they also fit the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max. The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Camera Control and Flex Stand has a clear back, a TPU frame, and a PU anti-yellowing coating. In simple terms, TPU is the flexible, shock-absorbing plastic used in most case frames, and it’s also what usually turns clear cases slightly yellow the longer you use them, so ESR adds a polyurethane (PU) coating to shield it. ESR upgraded the case’s UV protection for longer-lasting resistance to yellowing, and it’s SGS-certified for anti-yellowing. A clear case is supposed to show off your iPhone’s color, so staying clear longer is the whole point. The ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case with Flex Stand retains the same soft silicone leather and stain-resistant finish as the iPhone Duo version.

It has been revealed that on these models, the Flex Stand adjusts from 15 to 69 degrees for portrait and landscape viewing. That has you covered for StandBy mode on your nightstand and a show over your lunch break, with no separate stand to carry around.

Recent findings suggest that protection is where the two cases differ. ESR rates the Classic Hybrid for 4x military-grade protection with 16-foot drop protection, plus a full-coverage camera bar. The Atelier is rated for 3x military-grade protection, including 12-foot drop protection, and features a soft microfiber lining. Military-grade refers to the MIL-STD-810 drop test, which uses a 4-foot drop, so 4x and 3x mean ESR rates the cases for four and three times that height. Both include a built-in Camera Control cover and raised edges, and both use a precise magnetic ring layout that automatically aligns with MagSafe chargers, car mounts, wallets, and batteries.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case is up to 28% off, and the ESR Atelier Vegan Leather Magnetic Case is up to 37% off.

A case protects everything except the part you touch all day. The ESR UltraFit Armorite Pro Screen Protector covers the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, and the name is worth unpacking. Armorite is ESR’s line of toughened screen protectors, and the Pro version is made with Accessory Glass by Corning™. Corning has made the durable glass in Apple products since the very first iPhone, so in non-tech speak, this is glass from a trustworthy name rather than generic tempered glass.

Why it matters: ESR notes the protector delivers 10x the impact absorption of generic protectors, and Corning’s lab testing shows up to 2x better scratch performance and up to 25% less scratch visibility for its Accessory Glass. When you drop your iPhone or toss it in a pocket with your keys, the protector takes the hit instead of your screen. An anti-reflective coating reduces light reflection to just 2.3% while maintaining 94% optical transmittance, resulting in less glare outside and truer color. Edge-to-edge coverage leaves no gaps for dust to collect.

Installation is the part most people dread on a brand-latest iPhone, and ESR’s UltraFit tray handles it in two steps. Pull the tab, and the tray’s design clears dust and pushes out air bubbles as the glass goes down. Long gone are the days when you needed “professional installation” for a screen protector to look great.

Black Friday deal: The ESR UltraFit Armorite Pro Screen Protector is 15% off.

Holiday travel usually means one open outlet, an iPhone, a laptop, an e-reader, etc., that all need power, and cables left at home. The ESR Xtend 45W Retractable Charger builds the cable in. It has a braided cable that extends to 3.1 feet and fully retracts into the charger, and ESR rates it for 20,000 pulls and 10,000 bends. An extra USB-C port lets a second device charge simultaneously. 9to5Mac’s Michael Burkhardt went hands-on with the Xtend 45W earlier this month and said it’s an excellent iPhone fast charger on the go.

It’s rated at 45 watts and delivers up to 60 watts of dynamic power, enough to fast-charge phones and laptops, and it works with iPhone Duo, iPhone 15 through 18, and Android phones like Galaxy and Pixel. It supports PD 3.2 AVS, which in plain English means the charger and your device talk to each other, and the charger fine-tunes the power it sends to exactly what that device asks for. ESR states it can charge an iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max to 50% in about 15 minutes. It’s also TÜV-certified, meaning an independent testing organization has verified its safety features.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Xtend 45W Retractable Charger is up to 32% off from November 20 through December 1.

It has been revealed that for the student or anyone who does real work on an iPad, the ESR Shift Keyboard Case makes for an incredible gift. The Bluetooth keyboard attaches magnetically and comes off when you don’t need it, so you can type an essay at a desk, then pull the keyboard away to watch something on the couch or sketch with the iPad flat on a table.

Recent findings suggest that ESR built the Shift around five modes designed to make your iPad even more versatile. Productivity mode lets you detach the keyboard and type over Bluetooth, so the iPad can sit on a desk while the keyboard sits on your lap. Landscape mode adjusts from 20 to 75 degrees for typing and watching, Portrait mode holds 70 degrees for reading, browsing in Safari, or making a FaceTime call, and Drawing mode drops to a stable 20 degrees for sketching and editing with your Apple Pencil. Hands-On mode lets you hold the iPad like a regular tablet. An iPad is a laptop one minute and a tablet the next, and the Shift is designed to keep up with all of your iPad use cases.

For a student, that means taking notes in class with the keyboard attached, then detaching it to annotate a PDF or review flashcards on the couch. For someone who travels for work, it means answering email on a tray table, then pulling the keyboard off to watch a movie on the flight home. One case covers both, and the keyboard pairs and reconnects easily when you snap it back on.

Industry observers note that the trackpad is fully clickable and supports all the multi-touch gestures you already use on your iPad. Apple Pencil gets a home too. ESR’s Dual Smart Pencil Storage uses a magnetic holder and an elastic sleeve, so your Pencil stays with your iPad instead of rolling around the bottom of your bag. Its Air Guard corners protect your iPad when it’s stowed away.

The ESR Shift Keyboard Case comes in versions for iPad Pro 11-inch and 13-inch (M4 and M5), iPad Air 11-inch and 13-inch (including the latest M4 models), and iPad (A16), so whichever iPad you’re trying to take to the next level of productivity, there’s a Shift that fits it.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Shift Keyboard Case is up to 25% off, depending on your iPad model.

Have you ever dropped your AirPods case and watched the earbuds go flying? With the Cyber FlickLock, you won’t have to worry about that. We’ve covered FlickLock in MagSafe Monday before, but let’s recap it.

Recent findings suggest that when the internal latch is engaged, the magnets line up to attract each other and hold the lid shut with maximum force, adding a second layer of security. Slide the button, and the magnets shift to repel each other, so the lid pops open with one hand. ESR states the slide mechanism has been tested over 20,000 times.

Sources indicate that the result is that your AirPods stay in the case if you drop it. Both cases also have 260g of magnetic strength, so they snap onto MagSafe chargers, Apple Watch chargers, and MagSafe batteries if you need to charge your AirPods. Again, it’s extremely strong, but extremely easy to unlock with one hand.

The ESR Cyber FlickLock Magnetic Case is extremely durable and has a clip hook, so you can hang your AirPods on a backpack while hiking or cycling. The ESR Pulse FlickLock Magnetic Case brings the same lock in a range of vibrant colors with a carrying lanyard, so you can wear your AirPods on your wrist or attach them to a bag. Both cases come in versions for AirPods Pro 3, AirPods Pro 2 and 1, and AirPods 5 and 4. No matter which AirPods you or your loved one have, this is the case everyone will love.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Cyber FlickLock and Pulse FlickLock Magnetic Cases are both 20% off.

The ESR Equinox Watch Band is a quick pick for anyone who works out in the morning while tracking progress with Apple Watch, then heads to the office. A pin-and-fold lock keeps it secure, and it’s made from HNBR, a durable, skin-friendly synthetic rubber that resists water and tearing, with ventilation cutouts for all-day comfort. It fits 44mm, 45mm, 46mm, and 49mm models across Apple Watch Ultra 1 through 4, Series 4 through 12, and SE 1 through 3, and it comes in several colors to match your outfit or your mood that day.

Black Friday deal: The ESR Equinox Watch Band is 20% off.

The best gifts are the ones that get used every day, and accessories are the part of the Apple experience people live with the most. A case that props up a foldable, a screen protector made with Corning glass, a charger with a built-in cable, and an AirPods case that stays closed even when dropped check all the boxes. ESR truly makes something for everyone and is one of the most trusted names in the Apple accessories ecosystem.

ESR built its Black Friday lineup around the whole Apple ecosystem, from the fresh iPhone Duo to iPad, AirPods, and even a great Apple Watch band, with premium materials and versatile designs that are durable, functional, and great-looking. ESR’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals run on Amazon from November 19 through November 30 (the Xtend 45W runs through December 1), with discounts of up to 37%!

‘All of a Sudden’ Review: Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Long and Thoughtful Plea for a More Hopeful Future

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on May 15, 2026 during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Neon will release the film in limited theaters on Wednesday, November 25.].

A talky, female-driven, 196-minute drama about the infinitely braided relationship between care and capitalism that’s prone to Wiseman-like meeting scenes and frequent detours into the world of avant-garde theater? It almost feels redundant to say that Ryusuke Hamaguchi has returned.

And yet, for a movie that offers such an obvious continuation of his previous work (e.g. “Drive My Car,” “Happy Hour”), the sweet and stirring “All of a Sudden” also takes Hamaguchi to places his work has never gone before. Namely: Paris, where most of the Japanese filmmaker’s latest feature is set, but also — in an abrupt, almost contrite about-face from the environmental fatalism of 2023’s “Evil Does not Exist” — a palliative realm of pure comfort. Related Stories ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ Made Nearly $4 Billion Doing What Movies Can’t Frederick Wiseman’s Complete Filmography to Be Distributed by Janus Films.

There is much to mourn in this epic two-hander, which was inspired by the letters shared between terminal breast cancer patient Makiko Mayano and medical anthropologist Maho Isono, but few recent movies, or few movies at all, have been so rigorously insistent upon the reasons for hope. Indeed, “All of a Sudden” is centered around a scene in which the beautifully dying Mari — played by model and “Batman v. Superman: Dawn of Justice” actress Tao Okamoto, whose presence here at long last brings Hamaguchi’s films into the Snyderverse — literally diagrams the state of the world on a whiteboard. Her impromptu Ted Talk doesn’t solve for capitalism’s insatiable appetite, but it illustrates the problem with a clarity that makes a workable solution feel possible within our own lives, if maybe not in Mari’s own lifetime. And that is ultimately where Hamaguchi’s attention lies: In the pain and promise of conceding to the fact that so much is still possible for this world and its people, no matter how grim the prognosis.

In that light, it’s rather easy to appreciate why so (so) much of “All of a Sudden” is set in the memory care unit of a Paris nursing home, where the imperative for respectful treatment regularly butts up against the realities of dementia. Facility director Marie-Lou Fontaine (“Benedetta” star Virginie Efira) has made it her life’s work to reconcile those clashing forces as best as she can, but money talks, training is expensive, and the business model is biased towards the kind of care that keeps patients zombified in bed rather than encouraging them to engage with the world however they still can.

Proud of her burnout and happy to dismantle what little is left of her work/life balance (a mindset that Hamaguchi ultimately decides to support), Marie-Lou has begun the arduous process of training her staff in the ways of Humanitude, a tender but intensive French methodology that emphasizes dignity over death. While many of her colleagues support the idea in theory, even the most sympathetic among them struggle with the time and cost it has already taken to implement.

Recent findings suggest that effervescent despite its cloistered setting, much of this movie’s first hour is dedicated to the uneasy rhythms of life at the facility, where long — sometimes tempestuous — staff meetings alternate with living memorials, wherein Marie-Lou’s team works to remind their residents, their residents’ families, and themselves that even the most severe Alzheimer’s cases are still people who led full and vibrant lives. Such a pronounced decline makes it tempting to silo things into “before” and “after,” but Humanitude does what it can to stress that we all exist within a continuous “during.” Life, it maintains, persists until the moment it doesn’t. Even the most inevitable of deaths should feel as though it arrived… all of a sudden.

Despite his abiding fascination with artifice, Hamaguchi has always tended towards an unfussy aesthetic that see-saws between airy naturalism and Chekhovian melodrama, and — as if responding to the almost supernaturally heightened final moments of “Evil Does Not Exist” — “All of a Sudden” balances things back in the other direction. It would be reductive to say there’s never been less cinema in Hamaguchi’s cinema (many of the film’s more theatrical moments find a remarkable density within deceptively plain shots), but this movie, sterile by design, is very selective about how it deploys any self-insistent traces of romantic style or joie de vivre.

Which is to say that it feels like a real breath of fresh air when Marie-Lou is caught in a rainstorm after a chance encounter with a non-verbal Japanese teen named Tomoki (“Brand Fresh Landscape” actor Kodai Kurosaki), whose grandfather Goro (a wonderful Kyōzō Nagatsuka) is in Paris to perform a one-man show about the doctor who dismantled Italy’s abusive psychiatric system. Mari is the show’s director, and — in the most breathtakingly intimate moment of a film that has a few memorable ones to choose from — she and Marie-Lou bond during a post-performance Q&A in which the two women irritate the rest of the audience by having a heart-to-heart in Japanese.

According to recent reports, the Frenchwoman, we learn, spent time studying in Tokyo thanks to her love for Hayao Miyazaki and Isao Takahta (“even ‘Pom Poko!,’” she insists), and she’s instantly drawn in by Mari’s defiant attitude towards her cancer diagnosis. Goro’s show, which Tomoki interrupts whenever the mood strikes, maintains that only the dying are sensitive enough to appreciate the full scope of life’s beauty, and that message naturally resonates with the ethos of Marie-Lou’s approach to eldercare. So begins a whirlwind — and ostensibly platonic — affair between the French clinician and the Japanese director, who are soon walking along the Sienne à la “Before Sunset” and resigning themselves to the reality that work and pleasure are as inextricable from each other as late capitalism and population decline.

In a recent development, I’ll leave it to Mari to articulate the finer points of that argument (which she does with clarity and conviction), but the greater truth that her character allows Hamaguchi and co-writer Léa Le Dimna to postulate is that such clear separation between states of being — healthy as it might sound — makes it that much easier for l’argent to gobble them both up in its maw. “All of a Sudden” contends that there is life in work and work in life, and must be in order to prevent money from completely devaluing whatever portion of our minds and bodies that is no longer profitable. As capitalism plunders from the poor (and the natural world) in order to sustain the illusion of infinite growth, stealing from the future so as to protect the present, the conspiracy to maintain the status quo begins to exert an increasingly dehumanizing effect on those who dare to expose that everything isn’t hunky-dory after all.

The free markets have kept Mari alive for this long, but her body — like those of Marie-Lou’s patients — has become an inconvenient reminder of the fact that we’re all just one unfortunate diagnosis from being kicked out of the party. “Nowhere” and “now/here” (to use her chose terms) can’t be allowed to remain callously oppositional states. On the contrary, they have to be mixed together until the living are able to seize upon the unavoidable inevitability of death, and the dying are able to benefit from the enduring possibility of life. “Not inside and outside — we must mix everything together.”.

Sources indicate that heady and didactic as “All of a Sudden” so obviously is, Hamaguchi makes sure to embrace that ethos in his own right. While this movie is clearly segmented into three distinct acts (and further portioned between individual days of the calendar from there), the sense that it’s alternating between institutional and human dramas rewardingly gives way to the gradual dissolution of the space between those two modes. The scenes where Marie-Lou discusses Humanitude policy with her staff are increasingly freighted with real pathos, while the scenes where she and Mari grow closer to each other begin to have a practical effect on how things are done at the nursing home.

Just how much closer to each other Mari and Marie-Lou are willing to become remains something of an open question, but so it goes in a film where the distinction between friendship and romance is no more narrowly defined than anything else. Less interesting than the “will they/won’t they” of it all is the role that desire continues to play in these women’s lives. Sex is never an especially present concern, but Okamoto’s delicate and ethereal performance might have steered toward self-actualized hokum if not for she grounds it in the suggestion that Mari is left wanting more from Marie-Lou. Enchanted but not quite magical, the character remains just on the right side of believability, which is enough to stop her illness from seeming like a teachable moment (even if Efira’s wounded stoicism allows Marie-Lou to feel like a model student).

According to recent reports, even so, I was more emotionally involved by the concept of what Mari comes to represent than I was by the personal stakes of her cancer diagnosis, which lent a stifling kind of vertigo to the last act of Hamaguchi’s most overtly sentimental film to date. The story climaxes with a chaotic staging of Goro’s play, one that elegantly demolishes the line between viewers and participants — among other dichotomies — in order to stress that optimism and decline aren’t opposite forces, but “All of a Sudden” is so prescriptive with its ideas that its characters are liable to become vessels for them.

It’s the one regard in which Hamaguchi’s impulse to mash everything together softens the power of his point rather than sharpening it, and the one regard in which this three-and-a-half hour sit threatens to seem too short. Marathon-like as “All of a Sudden” might be, its message resonates so deeply because of the many elisions that it refuses to make, which leave the few handful of gaps in its timeline to feel like yawning chasms.

Of course, that’s a small criticism to level against a light and lovely movie that argues for a more humane future with the same conviction that “Evil Does Not Exist” articulated the glib destructiveness of our present. “All of a Sudden” may not resolve with the same visceral force as that film, or offer the richness of feeling that “Happy Hour” and “Drive My Car” earned by their ends, but it arrives at a power all its own through how credibly it grows more hopeful as it inches towards death. It makes the impossible seem possible.

“All of a Sudden” premiered in Competition at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. NEON will release it in theaters later this year.

Breaking: 10 'Find Hub' Hacks Every Android User Should Know

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1309 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Lifehacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that google's Find Hub app isn't just for tracking your lost smartphone.
  • This month, Google finally added Left Behind notifications to Android trackers—but you have to enable the feature manually.
  • In a recent development, there’s a hidden feature in the Find Hub app that helps you keep track of things without actually using a Bluetooth tracker.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that google's Find Hub app isn't just for tracking your lost smartphone. Over the past year, Google has consistently added features to manage your belongings, share your location with loved ones, and locate lost devices. Find Hub can now notify you when you've left your device or your tracker behind. Plus, you can use Gemini to remember where you left items, even without a tracker attached. Behind the scenes, there are even more hidden settings and features to help track your devices and make it easier to retrieve them in case they are stolen or misplaced. If you use Find Hub, you need to know about these 10 hacks.

This month, Google finally added Left Behind notifications to Android trackers—but you have to enable the feature manually. AirTags consumers should be familiar with this feature already. When you leave your tracker or device behind, and exit the location range, you’ll receive a notification that you left without your item. You need to enable this feature on a per-device basis. Go to Find Hub and select a device. Tap the settings gear icon next to the device's name, and enable Notify when left behind. While you’re here, go to Add location to add familiar locations where you don’t want to get a notification (like your home or workspace). Otherwise, Find Hub may spam you with left behind alerts.

In a recent development, there’s a hidden feature in the Find Hub app that helps you keep track of things without actually using a Bluetooth tracker. You can simply ask Gemini to remember where you put things, and it will show up in the Find Hub app. To use it, pull up Gemini and say something like, “Remember in Find Hub that the passport is in the downstairs wardrobe,” or “I’ve kept the spare car keys behind the garage door.”.

You can then ask Gemini, “Where did I keep my passport?” and it will tell you. If you change the location of an item, just ask Gemini to update it for you. When you go to the Remembered tab, you’ll see the location of all remembered items. You can also add items manually here using the Add button.

According to recent reports, some Android smartphones can remain findable for several hours after they've been switched off or their batteries have run out. If you’re using a supported device (like the latest Pixel series smartphone), you can use a hardware feature to track the location using Google’s mesh network, relying on nearby devices (similar to how Android tags work).

Recent findings suggest that to make sure this feature is enabled, go to Find Hub, and tap Find your offline devices. Here, make sure that either With network in busy places only or With network everywhere is selected.

It has been revealed that if you’re using a tracker in your car, luggage, or on your keys, you might want to share location access with your spouse or family members. Find Hub has a feature called "Share Ownership" that lets you share the tracker details with up to 10 people. Only the location of your tracker is shared, not your personal device.

To set it up, go to Find Hub, and choose the tracker or accessory that you want to share. Tap the Share Ownership button and follow the on-screen instructions to share the invite link via a messaging app or using Quick Share. Once the recipient taps Accept, you’ll get a notification. Go to the device settings in Find Hub and tap the Confirm button to enable location sharing.

Industry observers note that you can rapidly share your live location with your friends or loved ones using Google Messages. Open a conversation, tap the Attachment icon, and choose Real-time location. Set the duration and tap Send.

It has been revealed that if you don’t like using the Messages app, you can do so directly from Find Hub. Go to the People tab at the bottom of the screen, and tap the Plus icon. Choose the duration and select a contact to share the location with, then tap the Get Link button to copy the link. You can then share it via any messaging app of your choice.

It has been revealed that you might have a Find Hub tracker in your luggage to help keep tabs on your bags. But you don't have to be the only one privy to its location. If your airline loses that luggage, you can temporarily share its location with your airline to help you retrieve it. This is an official feature, too: Google partnered with multiple airlines to make this data sharing easier. From the Find Hub, choose your tracker. Tap the Share Item Location button, and then tap Share Item Location again. Copy the generated web link and share it with your airline using the app or support page. The link will automatically expire in seven days, so you don't have to worry about your airline continuing to monitor your luggage's location long after your flight.

Find Hub uses a mesh network of supported Android devices to securely locate your lost device or tag. But by default, it waits until multiple Android devices detect the location of the lost device. This works well if you've lost the device in crowded areas, but it can increase your wait time if you lose it somewhere remote. Luckily, there is a hidden setting that triggers location sharing even if a single device reports its location. Go to Settings > Google > All services > Find Hub > Find your offline devices and select With network everywhere instead of With network in busy places only.

If you’ve lost your smartphone, you don’t need to rush to a computer or a website to track it. Borrow someone’s Android smartphone and head into their Find Hub. Tap Sign in as guest and sign in with your Google account associated with your device, then find and select your device in the account. If requested, enter the PIN that you’ve previously set up. You can now track the device’s location, get directions to the device, or play a sound to help track the device if it’s nearby. If the device is truly lost, you can use the Mark as Lost feature to remotely lock your device.

Sources indicate that map-based tracking is helpful in getting to the general vicinity of your lost device. But your smartphone or tracker is hidden; finding it may require precision tracking. Many newer trackers like the Pixel Tag come with an ultra-wideband chip that helps you find the exact location of the tracker, given you are nearby. This also works on Pixel smartphones (Pixel 8 Pro series and above) and Samsung Galaxy devices (S21 and above, Plus and Ultra models only).

When using this feature, make sure you have Bluetooth enabled on your smartphone, then open Find Hub. Choose your tracker, and tap Find Nearby. Follow the on-screen instructions to locate the nearby device. You can also tap Play Sound to make the location process easier.

In a recent development, if you think your Android smartphone is lost or stolen, don’t rush to erase all data. While a remote factory reset is great for protecting your data, it also removes the device from your account. It’s best to try to get the device back. Two-factor authentication (or a passkey) on your Google account, along with a biometric lock on your smartphone, will protect the data itself.

It has been revealed that go to the Find Hub website, or use Find Hub on someone else’s phone in guest mode. Choose your device, and instead of Factory Reset, choose Mark as Lost. Here, you’ll see an option to enter a message. Type an alternative contact number, and a message to help recover the device.
