  • In a recent development, all eight episodes of "Blade Runner 2099" are available on Amazon Prime Video as of November 25, but what should you watch when you're finished with the series?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

"Blade Runner 2099" has finally premiered on Amazon Prime Video, and if you've been anxiously awaiting this entry in the storied sci-fi franchise inspired by Philip K. Dick's novel "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" (the basis for the property that debuted back in 1982 with Ridley Scott's "Blade Runner"), we've got great news for you. In his review for /Film, Bill Bria praised "Blade Runner 2099" (as was overseen by showrunner Silka Luisa), declaring that Silka "has put together something that's as unique and bold as it is in conversation with its franchise's past, making it a proud latest addition to the saga" and even calling the series "the best sci-fi show in years.".

Recent findings suggest that so, what's it about? "Blade Runner 2099," like its film predecessors "Blade Runner" and "Blade Runner 2049," focuses on the interplay between Replicants — an engineered humanoid — and Blade Runners, who are tasked with figuring out who's a human and who's a Replicant and disposing of the latter. (This is what Harrison Ford's Rick Deckard was doing, essentially, in "Blade Runner.") That's where we meet Olwen, a Replicant who's also a Blade Runner — played by Oscar winner Michelle Yeoh — and watch her team up with the human Cora (Hunter Schafer) in a post-revolution world where Replicants now control humans. As Olwen prepares to be retired and Cora pretends to be a Replicant, they look for a group of evil-doing Replicants causing chaos, allowing us to follow their adventures.

In a recent development, all eight episodes of "Blade Runner 2099" are available on Amazon Prime Video as of November 25, but what should you watch when you're finished with the series? I've got some ideas.

It has been revealed that despite ... diminishing returns as J.J. Abrams' show "Alias" reached its endpoint with its fourth season, I still hold this show close to my heart, and fans of the double-crossing and secret identities in "Blade Runner 2099" will definitely love this spy drama. When "Alias" opens, Jennifer Garner's Sydney Bristow is, by all appearances, juggling a high-pressure job at a Los Angeles bank with her graduate studies ... except, the truth is that she doesn't work at a bank but as a spy for what she believes is a covert wing of the CIA called SD-6. When she tells her fiancé the truth about her career and SD-6 has him brutally murdered in their home, Sydney realizes that SD-6 isn't affiliated with United States intelligence but is actually a terrorist cell that's part of a larger structure operating across the world. That's when Sydney becomes a double agent, teams up with her CIA handler (and future husband) Michael Vaughn (Michael Vartan), and works alongside the other mole inside SD-6 ... who turns out to be her estranged father Jack Bristow (a sublime Victor Garber).

Industry observers note that the first season of "Alias?" Amazing. The second season of "Alias?" God-tier television, especially "Phase One," the mid-season stunner that secured the coveted post-Super Bowl timeslot in 2003. Season 3 is where things start to go downhill, and in this house, we don't even discuss Season 4. Still, if you want to watch a few very good seasons of a spy drama after "Blade Runner 2099," check out "Alias," which is on Disney+.

Recent findings suggest that "Blade Runner 2099" is many things. "Good" is one of them. "Expensive" is definitely another. You can practically see dollar signs on the screen (the show just looks expensive, and I definitely don't mean that in a bad way). So, if you're looking for another major-budget sci-fi epic that's got plenty of seasons under its belt at this point, consider checking out the Apple TV show "Foundation." Adapted from Isaac Asimov's "Foundation" book series by David S. Goyer and Josh Friedman, "Foundation," which premiered in 2021 and stars Jared Harris and Lee Pace, takes place in a future where living beings live under the control of the Empire, led largely by clones (though it's secretly run by Laura Birn's Lady Demerzel, who controls all of the Empire's leader-clones). Pace plays Brother Day, a middle-era clone of Emperor Cleon I, while Harris plays mathematician Hariton "Hari" Seldon, who can predict the future and serves as a mentor to young prodigy Gaal Dornick (Lou Llobell).

In a recent development, "Foundation" is detailed, sumptuous, and again, looks expensive ... and whatever Apple is spending on this series is beyond worth it. Season 3 concluded in 2025 and the fourth season is already confirmed, so if you watch the show after "Blade Runner 2099," rest assured that there will be more "Foundation" on the way eventually.

The vibes of "Pluribus" and "Blade Runner 2099" couldn't be more different, but if you like the push-and-pull of the interplay between humans and Replicants in the latter, I bet you'll like the dynamic between a hivemind and an unsuspecting woman in the former. Vince Gilligan's first series since "Better Call Saul" reunites him with that show's lead actor Rhea Seehorn and casts her as Carol Sturka, a romance author who's understandably terrified when an alien virus turns almost every human on Earth into part of a hivemind except for her (including her manager/wife Helen L. Umstead, played by Miriam Shor). As one of 12 people immune to mentioned hivemind, Carol is at a total loss and absolutely refuses to follow the pack, which sets up a genuinely hilarious, deeply weird, and riveting series.

"Pluribus" won Seehorn her first-ever Emmy for playing Carol (well-deserved, especially after her years playing "Better Call Saul" lead Kim Wexler), and even though the series boasts a great ensemble, it's more or less a one-woman show as Carol moves through a completely changed Earth and tries to figure out her next move. If you haven't watched "Pluribus" yet and just finished "Blade Runner 2099," check this pick out.

"Blade Runner 2099" is a great series that happens to stand in the shadow of its predecessor, owing largely to the fact that "Blade Runner" is one of the most influential and beloved science fiction films of all time. This is also true of "Andor," an exceptional science fiction series that's part of a larger universe you might be familiar with called the "Star Wars" franchise. Created and run by the great Tony Gilroy, "Andor," a prequel to the movies "Rogue One: A Star Wars Story" and "Star Wars: Episode IV — A New Hope," centers on Cassian Andor (Diego Luna), a thief who becomes radicalized against the Galactic Empire over five years and ends up serving as an agent/spy for the Rebel Alliance.

Recent findings suggest that I probably don't need to tell you that "Andor" is one of the best Star Wars projects ever made (this is just established fact), but both "Andor" and "Blade Runner 2099" are given the daunting task of expanding a well-known universe in a way that doesn't feel like a stingy cash grab, and both succeed. If you haven't watched "Andor" yet, you're in for a serious treat. The show only runs for two seasons, but its sophomore outing is regarded as one of the best TV seasons in recent memory by pretty much all of its fans, and it really does pair perfectly with another legacy project like "Blade Runner 2099.".

If your favorite thing about "Blade Runner 2099" is the buddy aspect (namely, the way that Hunter Schafer and Michelle Yeoh's characters play against each other), consider another Amazon Prime Video series. Specifically, consider "Fallout," the adaptation of the blockbuster video game series that started airing on the streamer in 2024. The show, created by Graham Wagner and Geneva Robertson-Dworet (with Jonathan Nolan and Lisa Joy of "Westworld" among the executive producers), centers around Lucy (Ella Purnell), an individual who, like most other people in this world, lives in an underground bunker to avoid the nuclear aftermath of the Great War of 2077 between China and the United States. When Lucy's beloved father Hank is kidnapped suddenly from their home in Vault 33, she decides to venture to the surface and track him down ... and while there, she encounters The Ghoul, a former TV star named Cooper Howard who was mutated by the nuclear blast and is played by Walton Goggins.

It has been revealed that purnell and Goggins are an unexpectedly perfect duo, much like Yeoh and Schafer. So, again, if you're looking for a follow-up series to "Blade Runner 2099" that pairs two unlikely souls together and watches them embark on a journey, try the first two seasons of "Fallout" on Amazon Prime Video. That's also where you can find "Blade Runner 2099" — again, all of Season 1 is streaming now.

3 Reasons Why Console Prices Aren’t Going Down Anytime Soon

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (576 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At this point in a console generation, system prices would have usually come down significantly, broadening install bases and making gaming more accessible.
  • Unfortunately, that situation is unlikely to change anytime soon.
  • One of the main reasons consoles are so expensive right now is an ongoing shortage of hardware components needed to build these systems, specifically DRAM (memory).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At this point in a console generation, system prices would have usually come down significantly, broadening install bases and making gaming more accessible. That isn’t what happened this time around. The base PlayStation 5 costs $649.99, $150 more than at launch, while the Xbox Series X is $799.99, $300 more than when it came out six years ago.

Unfortunately, that situation is unlikely to change anytime soon.

One of the main reasons consoles are so expensive right now is an ongoing shortage of hardware components needed to build these systems, specifically DRAM (memory). This shortage has largely been caused by increased construction of AI data centers, which require vast quantities of memory. As per GameIndustry.Biz, an analysis by S&P Global Market Intelligence Kagan claims it will take until at least 2028 for console manufacturing prices to start coming down as DRAM production increases.

In a recent development, many major manufacturers have shifted from producing consumer-focused DRAM to the type of memory used in AI data centers, reducing the supply of consumer DRAM and causing prices to skyrocket. While manufacturers are looking to increase DRAM production to meet current consumer demand, it will reportedly take until 2028, at the earliest, for them to scale up. Beyond affecting the current generation of consoles, this will impact future consoles as well, meaning the next-gen Xbox Project Helix and PlayStation 6 would likely be exceedingly expensive if they were to launch next year.

Recent findings suggest that while current estimates indicate that prices for consumer DRAM could start coming down by 2028 due to increased production, much of this extra supply could end up going straight to AI data centers. “If data center demand grows, then it could promptly eat into the extra supply,” S&P analyst Neil Barbour stated to GamesIndustry.biz. “The memory [fabrication facilities] are not expanding with an eye specifically toward the consumer market. They’re racking up record revenue and margins on the data center build-out, so these supply expansions are primarily meant to feed that demand.”.

“However, if the build-out plateaus for regulatory reasons or simply because the demand isn’t as strong as they had anticipated, then more of that capacity could become available for traditional DRAM. What this data suggests is that the conversation doesn’t really even start until 2028.” If there’s a minor silver lining, Barbour adds, “I wouldn’t say further price increases are guaranteed in this environment.”.

On top of the ongoing DRAM shortage, the Trump administration proposed a newly introduced slate of tariffs on Wednesday, which will hit imports from dozens of countries, including China, Japan, South Korea, and members of the European Union. Many of the duties go up to 20 percent, and the administration threatened to raise tariffs on imports from China up to as high as 40 percent if Beijing doesn’t comply with certain demands.

A large share of the world’s RAM supply is produced by the South Korean companies Samsung and SK Hynix, as well as the Chinese firm CXMT. Samsung and SK Hynix primarily produce their RAM in China and South Korea. As for consoles, PlayStation 5s are manufactured in Japan, China, and other countries affected by U.S. tariffs. The Xbox Series consoles are also at least partially manufactured in China. Although it's hard to predict how long these duties will remain in effect, even if the Trump tariffs were lifted overnight, game console prices are likely to stay high for years to come.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping Explains One Haymitch Detail Nobody Ever Questioned

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" ahead.
  • It's obvious why prequels are appealing.
  • Sources indicate that in contrast, you have the "Hunger Games" film prequels, which actually flesh out the inhabitants and world of Panem in meaningful ways.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spoilers for "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" ahead.

It's obvious why prequels are appealing. After all, they allow you to see more of the characters you love in situations that are (hopefully) less miserable than the ones you previously saw them in. The problem with prequels is that they often offer origin stories and explanations for details that no one asked about. This is how we end up with stuff like, perhaps most infamously, the bizarre explanation for how Han Solo got his name in "Solo: A Star Wars Story.".

Sources indicate that in contrast, you have the "Hunger Games" film prequels, which actually flesh out the inhabitants and world of Panem in meaningful ways. Take "The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes," which is good enough to get you rooting for the "Hunger Games" franchise's major bad, Coriolanus Snow, as a young man despite knowing how monstrous he eventually becomes. It also reveals how the Games themselves came to be after nearly being canceled once upon a time. Notably, these explanations feel natural and crucial to the movie's story, as opposed to coming across as forced connections to the previous "Hunger Games" films.

The trend continues with "Sunrise on the Reaping," a fantastic movie that makes Haymitch Abernathy not only a hugely key character to the overall "Hunger Games" saga but one of its saddest, too. (If anything, this film shows he should be drinking more as an older man in the prior movies.) It even turns Plutarch Heavensbee into this franchise's version of Luthen Rael from "Andor," depicting him as a revolutionary stuck behind enemy lines and burning for a sunrise he'll never see.

And on top of all of that, it gives us the last backstory we expected — one for the gap in Haymitch's teeth when he's older.

Joseph Zada does a very good job in "The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping" as Haymitch, making the character his own to embody this particular period in the character's life. At the same time, he does capture a lot of Woody Harrelson's mannerisms as Haymitch from the original "Hunger Games" quadrilogy, including his voice. That being said, there is no denying that Zada does not look that much like Harrelson — especially with his curls and noticeable lack of a gap between his two front teeth, which is Harrelson's most distinguishable facial feature.

It has been revealed that however, rather than relying on viewers' suspension of disbelief, "Sunrise on the Reaping" actually closes the gap (pun intended) between the two actors. In the film, Haymitch is beaten within an inch of his life right before winning the titular Games, at which point he sets off an explosion as a final act of defiance. As a result, he's knocked unconscious, only to wake up later with his wounds having been stitched shut. Even so, he looks different now, with the impact of the explosion having broken his nose and smashed his teeth.

This is the "Hunger Games" equivalent of Hercule Poirot's mustache getting a gritty origin story tied to the horrors of WWI in Kenneth Branagh's "Death on the Nile" film adaptation, only here, it somehow works. It's because Haymitch examining his teeth is a blink-and-you-miss it detail, as opposed to one that the movie draws heavy attention to. Thus, there's no grand score announcing this as something important (like when River Phoenix's young Indy gets his scar and hat in "Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade"). Instead, it's simply showing the natural aftermath of a brutal fight.

Is it silly? Sure, but it works.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Rockford Files, one of the most beloved detective series in TV history, is returning to NBC in the Upcoming Year. David Boreanaz will step into the (gum)shoes of James Garner in the rebooted series. Jim Rockford was the only character who was set to return for the new series, but now we know that one of the most memorable characters from the original show is making a comeback.

It has been revealed that boreanaz stars as Jim Rockford, a detective who was framed for a crime he didn't commit. After a spell in jail, he's back on the streets to solve the cases of the downtrodden and the underdogs... for a reasonable fee, plus expenses. The series will also star Michaela McManus (Redux Redux), Ilfenesh Hadera (Godfather of Harlem), and Jacki Weaver (Silver Linings Playbook); it is showrun by Mike Daniels (Sons of Anarchy), who executive produces with Carl Beverly, Sarah Timberman, and David Hudgins.

It has been revealed that deadline reports that Brandon T. Jackson will recur on the new series, and his character should excite any old-school Rockford fans out there. He'll play Angel, a street hustler with a smart mouth who finds himself on the wrong side of a law. He turns to Rockford to clear his name, and soon finds a place in the detective's orbit. Jackson is an actor and stand-up comedian from Detroit, Michigan, who's starred in films like Tropic Thunder, Percy Jackson and the Lightning Thief, and I'm Beginning to See the Light. The series is set to premiere with a special preview episode on January 2, 2027, at 8 p.m. after NBC's NFL broadcast; it will then debut in its normal timeslot on Thursday, January 7, 2027, at 8 PM.

A great detective is really just a personality with a method attached, which is why we keep remaking the same four of them. Here is yours, what it says about you, and the case for them being the best in the business.

You let people think you are not a threat and then you simply never go away. Columbo is the only major detective show that tells you who did it in the first ten minutes, because the pleasure was never the puzzle, it was watching a rich man slowly realise he is in trouble.

You are the most interesting person in the room and you know exactly how to use it. Rian Johnson built Blanc as a gentleman detective who is also an outsider everywhere he goes, which lets him be charming at people who would never otherwise talk to him.

Everybody tells you everything, and you have never once asked them to. Jessica Fletcher is a crime novelist from a small town in Maine who is so warm and so obviously trustworthy that suspects confess to her essentially as a social courtesy.

You expect to be lied to and you are almost never disappointed. Chandler wrote Marlowe as a man with a rigid private code in a city that has none, which is why he takes the case, solves it, gets nothing out of it and takes the next one.

Played by Stuart Margolin (Death Wish), Evelyn "Angel" Martin was an associate of Jim Rockford's during his stint at San Quentin Prison. A small-time con man and grifter, Angel's scams constantly got him into trouble with the law or other criminals: trouble that Rockford often had to get him out of, usually at great risk to himself. First appearing in the pilot movie for the series, later renamed "Backlash of the Hunter," Angel would appear in several episodes each season and in all eight of the Rockford Files reunion movies. Paramount+ subsequently renewed the crime drama for its abbreviated fifth and final season, which the publication points out "was announced just days before the Netflix licensing deal was announced" that included the first four seasons of the series.

Latest Update: ‘Paper Tiger’: James Gray Convinced Adam Driver He Was Playing the Hero, Then Crafted His Mythic End

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Editor’s Note: The following story contains spoilers for “Paper Tiger.”.
  • One night, after his second child was born, James Gray found himself up late watching C-SPAN coverage of the Global Economic Forum in Davos, and saw something he held onto for years.
  • “This corporate CEO noted, ‘95% of people don’t know there’s a game, and they lose,'” said Gray on IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note: The following story contains spoilers for “Paper Tiger.”.

One night, after his second child was born, James Gray found himself up late watching C-SPAN coverage of the Global Economic Forum in Davos, and saw something he held onto for years.

“This corporate CEO noted, ‘95% of people don’t know there’s a game, and they lose,'” said Gray on IndieWire’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast. “Of the remaining 5%, 4% know there’s a game and don’t know how to play it, and 1% knows there’s a game and wins. And he said it with evident pride. I thought it revolting.”.

In a recent development, the CEO’s words hit home for Gray, showing a “cruel economic system that people can’t control,” where luck, timing, and “having skills that are popular at the right time” decide who wins. Related Stories ‘All of a Sudden’ Review: Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Long and Thoughtful Plea for a More Hopeful Future ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ Made Nearly $4 Billion Doing What Movies Can’t.

Sources indicate that “I would love a system where everyone got rewarded, not one that picks winners and losers,” said Gray. “The idea of losers breaks my heart. The film was about my heartbreak over the world’s losers.”.

Recent findings suggest that the script for “Paper Tiger” centers on three lead characters, each representing a different side of Gray’s cautionary tale about the dangers of chasing the American Dream. Of his three main characters, Gary (Adam Driver) is best positioned to be one of the “winners.”.

Industry observers note that “[Gary] is the one person who knows the game, knows how to play it, and just [can’t] live with himself if he makes certain choices that might allow him to, quote-unquote, ‘win,’” mentioned Gray of Driver’s character. “We don’t see that much in movies. We see people who are ‘bad guys’ who make the wrong choice, or ‘good guys’ who make the right choice and then wind up winning for it.”.

Gary, the ex-cop turned savvy businessman, presents himself as comfortable crossing that ethical line, but as the story slowly reveals, a strong moral code lies beneath Gary’s slick, tailored suit and wheeler-and-dealer image. It’s a distinction Gray noted Driver didn’t fully grasp at first.

“I would go up to [Adam’s] apartment, and we would talk about it, and I remember he was struggling and struggling and struggling, ‘Oh, what am I doing?’” said Gray. “One day in rehearsals, I said, ‘He has only the best intentions all the time. We have to love him. He always means well. He’s not a sleazeball.’ And Adam went, ‘Oh, I got it.’”.

Part of Driver’s problem was that Gary’s latest scheme places his brother Irwin (Miles Teller) and his family in the crosshairs of ruthless Russian mobsters, but Gray warned it was crucial, for both Driver and the audience, to understand that Gary’s actions weren’t particularly reckless at the time.

“We have the wisdom of 2026 about where organized crime would go in New York, but in 1986, the Russian organization was a totally unknown quantity,” said Gray. “He would not, as a retired police officer, have any knowledge of that.”.

Recent findings suggest that in 1986, the Italian mob’s stranglehold on the Gowanus Canal — where Gary is trying to help Irwin score a lucrative contract as an environmental consultant — had been decimated by RICO prosecutions. There was an assumption of a upcoming day dawning, as different immigrant groups began moving into the vacuum left behind by the aggressive prosecution of the Genovese crime family. No one imagined, according to Gray, that one mob would ultimately be replaced by a far more violent and ruthless mob altogether.

Sources indicate that “The sadness to me was that the story of immigration in Fresh York at that time was, ‘Oh, these are dissidents, these are engineers, they’re scientists, they’re doctors.’ The expectation wasn’t they were going to set up gasoline, oil, and racketeering. None of that was on the plate,” stated Gray, before connecting his point back to Driver. “Adam had the key now that everything was not done for nefarious reasons, that he was trying to bring his brother along. As soon as he could approach it that way, it really opened things up for him.”.

Much like the rest of the world, the ruthlessness of the Russian mob would catch Gary by surprise, but it would be how Gary responded to the threat that got Gray’s storytelling juices flowing.

“I was anxious to show a character who you might think would be the one who does the wrong thing, but in fact, does something beautiful in death, which is he sacrifices himself,” remarked Gray.

Sources indicate that this last part is notable to Gray, who discussed how his three young adult children constantly complain that “there’s nothing on TV,” despite having more channels and streaming services than ever before. “They always say that to me,” explained Gray, “and what they’re really saying is there’s very little with a streak of grandeur or nobility in it, because there’s a kind of smallness to the storytelling when you don’t have that quality.”.

Sources indicate that the question then became how to give Driver’s Gary that nobility in death, and build to a third act that gave Gray’s smaller film a sense of grandeur. As with most of his films, Gray drew on his life experiences growing up in Queens, along with great films from the past.

In Howard Beach, Queens, down by JFK Airport, a long stretch of marshes surrounded by tall reeds (phragmites grass) stands in sharp contrast to the urban landscape on the horizon.

“ My brother and I got lost in these very tall weeds,” said Gray. “I was very young. And it’s a recurring nightmare of mine, getting lost in there. And you have no sense of direction. Immediately, it’s extremely disorienting.”.

Industry observers note that gray had tried to use the location in his 2007 film “We Own the Night,” but he wasn’t satisfied with the results. In “Paper Tiger,” he cracked how to stage and shoot in the tall grasses, drawing direct inspiration from Masaki Kobayashi’s 1967 “Samurai Rebellion,” resulting in Gary’s last stand being one of the most memorable sequences in recent American movie memory.

In a recent development, A key was how Gray drew meaning from the setting: “I was trying to give Adam Driver‘s character a nobility, but the other part of it is how do you give his character a mythic dimension? And through death, a lot of the times, you can imply transcendence, and I was trying to say that his character was essentially going back to the primordial ooze, that he was returning to something that had nothing to do with the urban landscape.”.

Industry observers note that on the podcast, Gray talked about how the final scene is stripped of period signifiers, with no glimpse of the urban landscape beyond the weeds, allowing the sequence to “devolve or evolve so that [Gary] would be at peace as he died.” The moment was further brought to life through an effective use of sound, rather than a more traditional score for such an operatic ending. “I just decided this is about him transcending, and so you hear — the track is very weird — birds and insects. There’s the intrusion of aircraft, but it’s also the calm of the wind and the undulation of the phragmites grass. And I just thought that was a way to separate his character and say that he’s reached a kind of mythic status.”.

One lesson Gray took from his previous (and in Gray’s mind less successful) attempt to film in the Howard Beach marsh was that he would need more time for the hot and hellish shoot, in which the filmmakers experienced disorientation not unlike Gray did as a kid.

Sources indicate that “There’s one shot which is up high where you see these guys converging on Adam’s character. And I remember how difficult the shot was because the minute you put the actor in there and the camera went up here, we couldn’t find the actors in the weeds,” said Gray. “It’s very upsetting and disorienting even to just shoot in that setting, to say nothing of the ticks. But that’s a whole other story.”.

“Paper Tiger” expands nationwide on November 25.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that to no one’s surprise, Mario Kart World remains the best-selling game on the Nintendo Switch 2, with an impressive 16.48 million copies sold. When you consider that there are only around 26.35 million Switch 2 owners total, that means almost 63 percent of Switch 2 players have a copy of Mario’s latest kart racer. It's a somewhat staggering figure, given that the game costs $79.99.

Now, more than a year after its release, Nintendo is bringing upcoming courses and fan-requested features to the Switch launch game.

Nintendo released the latest update for Mario Kart World on Tuesday, and players have responded to it well. Ver 1.9.0 is a free update that adds eight remixed tracks, among other changes. The updated courses use a somewhat hilarious naming convention of slapping a 2 onto the end of each stage name. As a Redditor explained, there are basically three types of course remixes included: reverse variants, entirely upcoming track layouts, and an existing path made into its own track. Specifically, Salty Salty Speedway 2, Mario Bros Circuit 2, and Airship Fortress 2 are new tracks with reused assets; DK Pass 2, Wario Stadium 2, Desert Hills 2, and Koopa Troopa Beach 2 are reverse variants; and Shy Guy Bazaar 2 turns an existing path into its own track.

It has been revealed that beyond the remixed courses, the patch also adds two newly introduced routes for Knockout Tour mode, in which racers compete until only one is left standing. There’s Feather Rally, which connects Mario Bros Circuit to Boo Cinema, and Lucky Cat Rally, which links Question Block Ruins to Sky-High Sunday.

Lastly, 1.9.0 brings an enhanced Replay feature that lets you view past races and battles, so you can relive that time you were in first until you got hit by a blue shell, Bullet Bill, and a lightning bolt.

Sources indicate that unlike some of Mario Kart World’s updates, fans have responded well to the game’s latest patch. “This was a great update and adds more variety to the game’s track selection while being free DLC. I actually can’t wait to see more for it,” one Redditor wrote. Another user commented, “This is a great format for an update- 8 upcoming tracks (with a combination of reverse and new layouts) and 2 new tour rallies. They should have been doing this every 3 or 4 months after release, in my opinion.”.

In a recent development, despite Mario Kart World’s impressive sales figures and generally positive reviews, the game has divided its player base due to certain design decisions. Specifically, many players disliked that the game’s online mode featured interconnecting highways (called intermissions) as race destinations instead of traditional tracks, something Nintendo still hasn’t fixed. Hopefully, this latest revision indicates the game is trending back in the right direction and that a more fundamental rework is on the way.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Warning: This article contains major spoilers for the Season 3 finale of "The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power.".

Well, that was anticlimactic ... or was it? For much of "The Rings of Power" Season 3, we've been bracing ourselves for the onset of open war. Sauron's (Charlie Vickers) forces, bolstered by the hordes of followers loyal to the Dark Wizard (Ciarán Hinds) in Rhûn, have had their eyes on conquering Middle-earth. Even before the Dark Lord forged his One Ring, victory seemed all but certain. And, in the finale, the arrival of the Númenórean army in support of the Elves finally appeared to give us the epic battle we've been building towards all along. Instead, Sauron opts for the most shocking choice imaginable: He takes off his One Ring, kneels before King Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle), and surrenders himself to his enemies without a fight.

Recent findings suggest that unless this is your first encounter with Sauron the Deceiver, of course, it's plain to see that he has plans within plans. While the details of this particular one are left entirely off-screen (we only see him look meaningfully at the approaching army and presumably inform Tyroe Muhafidin's Nazgnagôl Theo of his intentions), there's one revealing moment that tells us all we need to know. Inspired by Elrond's wisdom (Robert Aramayo) and his insistence that death is not a curse but a gift, the Men of the West begin chanting in the language of Quenya. Sauron translates for his puzzled ally: "They're asking for death." And while Theo wants to grant their request through battle, Sauron calmly implies that he has a different scheme in mind.

With just a single exchange, "The Rings of Power" perfectly tees up what's to come in Season 4.

Did you catch the subtext dripping from Sauron's words? If not, be aware that the rest of this article will contain spoilers for what's to come in Season 4 of "The Rings of Power." For the book readers, we know it all has to do with this year's season-long interest in mortal Men. Remember that conversation between Elrond and his twin brother Elros in Episode 5, when Elros revealed that he'd chosen mortality as a human over an unfathomably long life as an Elf? Elrond couldn't understand this pivotal decision then, but he's since come to understand why the godlike Valar intended this as a "gift" rather than a "doom." Between the tragedy of surprising main character Eärien (Ema Horvath) in choosing a quick death over a life of torture, the bittersweet hopes of lovers Míriel (Cynthia Addai-Robinson) and Elendil (Lloyd Owen) reuniting in the afterlife, and Elrond grappling with his own grief over his brother, we've seen numerous instances proving that death need not be the worst outcome.

So, perhaps it was only a matter of time before Sauron reached a similar conclusion. Having witnessed the Númenórean soldiers publicly embrace the concept of death, as the Faithful have always done, the Dark Lord smirks to himself and promises to give them what they ask ... just not in the way they think. Indeed, as we know from the canon, Sauron's abrupt surrender is exactly what goes down in J.R.R. Tolkien's original writings. In the face of overwhelming numbers, the Dark Lord allows himself to be captured and brought back to the island kingdom of Númenór, where he immediately begins causing mischief that ends in disaster.

Sources indicate that yeah, you probably knew where this was headed. Ever since Season 1, "The Rings of Power" has been teasing the inevitable fall of Númenór. Like Atlantis, Rome, or any number of haughty civilizations before it (both real and mythological), this empire of Men has been doomed to be humbled from the moment Galadriel (Morfydd Clark) first washed up on their shores with Sauron (then disguised as Halbrand). Even before Season 3 ramped up the conflict between the two enemy factions fighting for control of the island, the cracks in the foundation had been very apparent. And, in a bold choice, showrunners J.D. Payne and Patrick McKay haven't shied away from that, even giving Míriel visions of a "great wave" consuming them all back in Season 1.

According to recent reports, well, we're now right on track for this worst case scenario. With Sauron on his way and with every intention of putting the arrogant Pharazôn (Trystan Gravelle) in his place, expect yet another storyline where the Dark Lord manipulates one of our main protagonists — first with Galadriel, then the Elven smith Celebrimbor (Charles Edwards), and, most recently ,Celeborn (Jamie Campbell Bower). How, you ask? Well, it has to do with Númenór's proximity to the Undying Lands to the west. Once these Men begin looking towards the Valar with envy at their immortality, encouraged by Sauron himself, it takes very little effort to imagine Pharazôn leading his forces against these godlike beings ... and paying the ultimate price for it.

Yeah, fans are going to want to stick around for everything to come in Season 4. All eight episodes of "The Rings of Power" Season 3 are now streaming on Prime Video.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Alien invasion highlights have been a staple of television for decades, with everything from the procedural thrills of The X-Files to the original V series to Futurama giving viewers a look at what could happen if such visitors were among us.
  • Industry observers note that resident Alien sadly wrapped up in 2025, sending off its ensemble in a touching and bittersweet finale that emphasized character development above all else.
  • In a recent development, making viewers care about the trials of Harry is one of Resident Alien’s best moves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alien invasion highlights have been a staple of television for decades, with everything from the procedural thrills of The X-Files to the original V series to Futurama giving viewers a look at what could happen if such visitors were among us. Every series took its own look at what the aliens were about, and how their specific goals influenced the humans in their orbit. Even the 1980s sitcom ALF followed a refugee from the planet Melmac seeking family and connection in the suburbs. Aliens in these shows might be threatening, seemingly benevolent, or wholly focused on dominating humanity. One show that split the difference was Syfy’s Resident Alien, the ALF-esque tale of an alien who crash-lands into the small mountain town of Patience, Colorado.

Industry observers note that resident Alien sadly wrapped up in 2025, sending off its ensemble in a touching and bittersweet finale that emphasized character development above all else. But across its four seasons, it ran the full scope of alien storylines, with its fish-out-of-water saga of Harry Vandespiegle (Alan Tudyk) becoming enmeshed in the drama of Patience’s citizens functioning as an engine for a much bigger story. A mysterious connection to a child who sees through Harry’s disguise? Decades-long plans from villainous “Greys” who plot to harvest human souls? Full-time alien investigators on Earth who wrestle with their own traumatic backstories? Using these tropes made for a stronger show, one that could be genuinely compelling while also having a lot of heart.

In a recent development, making viewers care about the trials of Harry is one of Resident Alien’s best moves. Operating on the ALF playbook, the show gets pathos and humor out of its protagonist’s difficult attempts to understand what humanity even is. Where ALF (a nickname meaning Alien Life Form) followed Gordon Shumway, or just ALF (puppeted and performed by Paul Fusco), an alien from the planet Melmac who crash-landed on Earth, Resident Alien’s Harry is going through a similar journey, with a major difference: ALF can’t change his appearance, and Harry is essentially using a human meatsuit. As well, Harry loves Law and Order, while ALF is obsessed with a polka TV show. ALF is particularly edgy for an '80s family sitcom, navigating a balancing act of its own while being infamous for one of the most shockingly bleak series finales of its genre.

Sources indicate that that show practically set the stage for American Dad’s Roger Smith (Seth MacFarlane) as an alien in hiding. Resident Alien doesn’t quite go to that series’ ‘90s sitcom level of coziness. While ALF was willing to deal with its lead’s isolation while living with the Tanner family, it still had a breezy California sweetness reflective of its era. Episodes like the one where ALF befriends a blind woman by calling into the radio embody some of the heart that Resident Alien would pick up on. Resident Alien’s easygoing qualities owe a lot to ‘90s television, ultimately landing somewhere between ALF and Northern Exposure, but it’s to the show’s credit that it was also able to adopt a lore that was also very engaging.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to long-running reveals that ultimately concerned themselves with an alien invasion storyline, Resident Alien owes a great deal to the slow burn of The X-Files as well. While The X-Files was a wildly entertaining procedural show that could follow its leads, Mulder (David Duchovny) and Scully (Gillian Anderson), on a fresh investigation every week (sometimes even dealing with true stories), it did gradually build up its mythology of government conspiracies and colonizing aliens working with humans to plot their eventual world domination. The X-Files mytharc is maybe less popular these days than singular individual powerhouse episodes (the Emmy-winning one where Peter Boyle plays a man who can see when people die is just a case-of-the-week episode), but there’s no denying its influence, especially on Resident Alien.

Resident Alien’s great strength is in synthesizing both its good-natured sitcom side with the deeper, conspiratorial arc of its overall story. What it borrows from The X-Files (alien colonists, government cover-ups, incredible work from Terry O’Quinn), it incorporates alongside stories of the larger ensemble of Patience. The overarching plot of the Resident Alien’s evil Greys serves as a mythological anchor for all four seasons. But as tends to be the case with shows like Resident Alien, what keeps audiences coming back to it is the strength of the characters, and our investment in their lives. Harry has the sweetness and soul of ALF within the larger conflict of The X-Files, and that combo turns the show into something very rewarding.

Industry observers note that lauren Ambrose sounds almost embarrassed to admit that she was puzzled the first time she read the script for Nick Payne’s “The Unbelievers.” “I was like, ‘Oh my God, what is this? I don’t understand this at all,'” Ambrose told IndieWire, scrunching up her face in a mask of bewilderment. “What’s he getting at?”.

The drama, which is wrapping up its limited run at the Manhattan Theatre Club this month, is elliptical, moving backward and forward in time as it follows Miriam’s search for her missing son, Oscar. That description sounds like a thousand thrillers, but “The Unbelievers” resists easy classification — it’s a narratively daring story, overflowing with ideas about grief and faith and family. Related Stories ‘Paper Tiger’: James Gray Convinced Adam Driver He Was Playing the Hero, Then Crafted His Mythic End ‘All of a Sudden’ Review: Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s Long and Thoughtful Plea for a More Hopeful Future.

Sources indicate that it was only after doing a workshop for the play that Ambrose discovered that what she initially found so alienating about “The Unbelievers” was actually its greatest strength. “There’s a lot to talk about, and a lot to parse, and a lot to think about, and it’s highly interpretable and analyzable, and I think that’s actually a marker of good art is that it can be interpreted in many ways,” Ambrose said over Zoom, hours before she was set to take the stage again.

The role of Miriam is almost Everest-like in its difficulty. As the years pass without any sign of Oscar — not knowing if he’s been kidnapped or murdered or ran away — Miriam becomes more obsessed, more unmoored by the lack of resolution. That strains her relationship with her two daughters and Oliver’s father, who are processing their grief in different ways and worry that Miriam is growing fanatical in her insistence that he may still be out there.

Sources indicate that “It’s fun in a perverse way to go on this crazy journey every night,” Ambrose remarked. “There are all these wild turns. It’s tiring vocally. My body hurts, my neck is messed up. But it’s amazing to get to play a part like this. You just have to throw yourself off a cliff.”.

Ambrose made a name for herself in films like “Can’t Hardly Wait” and on “Six Feet Under,” where she played Claire Fisher, a rebellious dreamer growing up in her family-run funeral home. The show debuted in 2001 on HBO, where it aired alongside “The Sopranos” and “Sex and the City” at the peak of the cable channel’s cultural supremacy. Decades later, “Six Feet Under” has been rediscovered on streaming by Gen Z, giving it an unexpected surge in popularity.

Sources indicate that “It was a golden age,” Ambrose remarked. “We were making these hour-long films each week. And HBO was so open and supportive of creative people. The attitude was, if you want to try something, try it. There weren’t algorithms determining everything. That freedom is palpable with the series, so I think that’s why it’s resonating and why it’s being embraced by this new generation.”.

Ambrose remains in demand on the big and small screen, recently appearing on another water-cooler hit, Showtime’s “Yellowjackets.” But she’s made a point of returning to the stage throughout her career, appearing on Broadway in “Exit the King” and “Awake and Sing!,” as well as earning a Tony Award nomination playing Eliza Doolittle in a revival of “My Fair Lady.”.

In a recent development, “I love the stage — I love it so much,” Ambrose said. “I love a rehearsal room. It’s my favorite place in the world. It’s where you’re figuring it out and making connections. But a play is always a living thing. We’ve opened ‘The Unbelievers,’ but I haven’t stopped my work of trying to scavenge around and figure out this mysterious character.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The future of Doctor Who may still be uncertain, but now Billie Piper is revealing the real reason she originally left the franchise.
  • When the BBC revived the sci-fi series with Christopher Eccleston, Piper was cast as the fresh Doctor Who companion.
  • Now Piper is opening up about her reason for initially leaving Doctor Who after appearing in only two seasons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The future of Doctor Who may still be uncertain, but now Billie Piper is revealing the real reason she originally left the franchise.

When the BBC revived the sci-fi series with Christopher Eccleston, Piper was cast as the fresh Doctor Who companion. She stayed on when David Tennant took over the lead role but left after season 2. Over the years, Piper has made additional appearances, including in season 4 with David Tennant, the 2010 Christmas special and the 50th anniversary special.

Now Piper is opening up about her reason for initially leaving Doctor Who after appearing in only two seasons. While speaking with Collider, she admitted that she wanted to depart after just one season because of Eccleston's exit, which "felt quite destabilizing," and she was ready to play other characters.

At the time, Piper was in her early 20s, and her mindset was that she didn't want to have the responsibility or the pressure of being a role model because she was "wild" and "it just felt like the two things were completely at odds.".

Doctor Who is a very popular and beloved series, which meant Piper became famous on a level she had never experienced before (even as a singer), which she didn't like.

At the end of the day, leaving Doctor Who was a "really easy decision for me," and she didn't care what other people thought about her choice since she knew herself better than anyone and what was best for herself.

It has been revealed that billie Piper: "[I was] wanting to leave after season 1. Mostly, that was a bit reactive because Chris [Eccleston] was leaving and that felt quite destabilizing, but I wanted to move on with what I wanted to play. And that, I think, I have always been quite headstrong about. I didn’t want to be on a family show anymore. I really didn’t like the feeling of the role model responsibility. I really didn’t like that pressure because I was in my early 20s, and I was wild, so it just felt like the two things were completely at odds, and I didn’t like carrying that. I didn’t like how famous it made me, again, in the UK, having done my teens as a singer. So it was a really easy decision for me. So it sort of was irrelevant what other people said. And then I’ve done that a few times in my career. So in that sense, I sort of feel like I know my mind that much. My issue is saying no to, like, I don’t know, hours or places I’ve got to go, or just stuff. The minutiae of it, really.".

Before Doctor Who's revival, Piper was both an actor and a singer, and released two albums in 1998 and 2000. After leaving the series, Piper went on to appear in films like City of Tiny Lights and Catherine Called Birdy, and the TV demonstrates Secret Diary of a Call Girl, Penny Dreadful and Wednesday.

Sources indicate that she also directed and wrote the script for Rare Beasts and co-created I Hate Suzie. Piper's most recent project is the upcoming biopic Elsinore, which was just released in U.S. theaters and has earned positive reviews from critics and audiences alike.

According to recent reports, piper made a shocking appearance at the very end of the Doctor Who season 15 finale when Ncuti Gatwa's Doctor regenerated into her character. The fandom had a lot of questions after that cliffhanger, and the assumption was that everything would be clarified in the subsequent season.

It has been revealed that unfortunately, the franchise has experienced a lot of turbulence since then, most notably when Disney pulled out of its partnership with the BBC. Lower ratings could no longer justify the expensive production costs associated with Doctor Who. Showrunner Russell T. Davies left the show, as did Gatwa.

According to recent reports, the BBC eventually declared it would undergo a competitive tender to secure a fresh production company. The endeavor got underway several weeks ago, and various studios and producers submitted proposals, including Jed Mercurio's Hat Trick, World Productions, STV Studios and a label associated with BBC Studios.

Interviews with each finalist will take place in early 2027, and one will be chosen in March. The blueprint is to get Doctor Who back on the air in 2028 or 2029.

It's unclear if Piper will return to Doctor Who in any capacity to continue or otherwise explain her appearance in the 2025 finale.

Doctor Who follows the Doctor and their companion as they journey across time and space, encountering a range of extraordinary friends and adversaries, expanding the universe of the long-running British science fiction series.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo have been out for quite some time now, and despite that, it’s still incredibly challenging to order an iPhone Duo in a timely manner. If for whatever reason you’re considering skipping out on this year’s iPhones, here’s what you have to look forward to next year.

2027 is going to be a relatively big iPhone release year for Apple. First, the manufacturer will be continuing the iPhone 18 lineup after it introduced a split release schedule. Then, in the fall, the company will debut a newly introduced round of flagships in celebration of the 20th anniversary of the iPhone. Here’s what to expect.

For the first time, Apple will be introducing its base iPhone in the spring. Upgrades for the iPhone 18 aren’t quite clear, though more RAM is one of the key rumors. Thermal upgrades will likely happen as well, as well as the new Apple C2 modem.

It’s possible Apple will patch the design to fall more in line with the iPhone 17 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro, though we don’t yet know.

This phone will of course equip the A20 chip, and it’ll probably start at the same $899 price point that iPhone 17 presently sits at – after it was increased from $799 in September.

This phone will most likely just end up being a chip bump from the A19 to A20 chip, and debut in the Spring alongside the iPhone 18. Earlier this year, reports indicated that Apple would share many components between the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e, though it isn’t quite clear what that could mean for the devices.

Out of all of the spring iPhone releases, this one is the one to look forward to. After receiving a lukewarm reception with the initial iPhone Air model, Apple went back to the drawing board and decided to modify the design to fit an ultrawide camera into the device.

Recent findings suggest that personally, I don’t think an ultrawide camera is too important – though many people will see one camera on the back of the phone and immediately assume it’s less premium, so it’ll probably end up being an important upgrade for the sake of sales. Plus, ultrawide photos can be fun at times.

It should also have a larger battery, reportedly as large as 3500mAh. That’s a roughly 10% improvement from the original iPhone Air. iPhone Air 2 will likely also jump from Apples C1X modem to the C2.

For the 20th anniversary of the iPhone, Apple is expected to debut a fully redesigned iPhone to celebrate. It’ll reportedly be much more glassy, feature significantly slimmer bezels, a quad curved display, and ditch the flat edge design of the iPhone 12 and later.

Industry observers note that personally, I’m slightly skeptical that this’ll truly be a replacement to the “Pro” phone for thermal reasons, but time will tell. iPhone Duo seemingly has strong thermals while not featuring an aluminum unibody, so my concern might not be relevant. It’ll offer two, larger display sizes: 6.4-inch and 7-inch. This largely comes from the bezel reduction.

Industry observers note that I wish they prioritized the Telephoto camera more. I need that (whether it be on an Air or a Duo) way more than an Ultrawide.

If you’re holding out for iPhone 18 Pro, this “iPhone 20” is definitely the phone to wait out for.

Lastly, Apple will release a successor to its just-confirmed iPhone Duo next fall. Of course, you can expect next-generation Apple Silicon with the A21 Pro chip next year, but there aren’t many other substantial changes expected. Apple may bring proper Face ID to the outer display, an improvement from the recently-announced face unlock, but it’s unclear whether this feature will make the engineering cutoff date.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite latest competition, the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5 remains one of the most efficient, well-rounded electric crossovers you can buy. While its cabin styling is starting to feel a bit dated, its standout real-world efficiency and spacious interior gives it broad appeal.

Efficiency improves in a big way.

Plenty of legroom and trunk space.

Sharp 360-degee cameras make parking a breeze.

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

In a recent development, I first got into the driver’s seat of the Ioniq 5 a couple of years back and came away impressed by its futuristic aesthetics and loaded suite of tech features that really added value to its bottom-line cost. At the time, it stood out as one of the easiest electric crossovers to recommend, easily one of the best electric cars for the money.

In a recent development, fast-forward to today, and I feel a bit differently after driving more than 80 EVs this year alone. While there's more competition in the compact crossover SUV segment now than ever, car shoppers can’t overlook the $50,815 as-tested price attached to the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5 AWD Limited I tested.

Sure, I’ve driven compelling rivals like the Ford Mustang Mach-E, Kia EV6, and the newer Subaru Trailseeker, but you can’t count out the Ioniq 5 just yet. Here’s why.

According to recent reports, I drove the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5 for a total of 142.3 miles, reaching an impressive 3.9 mi/kWh throughout that time. Not only is that a marked improvement over the 3.3 mi/kWh average I got when I tested the 2024 model, but it also easily outpaces rivals like the 2026 Subaru Trailseeker and the 2027 Rivian R2.

Recent findings suggest that the Ioniq 5 really shines around town, hitting mostly local roads with stop-and-go traffic and reaching a peak short-distance efficiency of 5 mi/kWh. On longer highway drives, it’s still pretty efficient with a best output of 3.8 mi/kWh. This improvement is important because while Hyundai rates it for 259 miles on a full charge, my 3.9 mi/kWh average translates to roughly 328 miles of real-world range from its 84 kWh battery.

According to recent reports, unfortunately, I couldn’t charge it at home because it didn’t come with a charger, nor did I have an adapter to connect my older J1772 charger. Despite this, adopting Tesla’s NACS charging port makes public charging far more accessible — and Hyundai claims it can add 178 miles of range in just 15 minutes on a 350kW DC fast charger.

2026 Subaru Trailseeker Touring.

Best long distance driving efficiency.

Best short distance driving efficiency.

In a recent development, one of the biggest surprises during my week with the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5 wasn't just how smoothly it drove — it was how little energy it used doing it. Again, I can’t stress enough how impressive the 3.9 mi/kWh overall average is, which puts it squarely among the most efficient electric crossovers in its class, especially for a dual-motor AWD model.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Usually, hitting numbers near the 4 mi/kWh mark is reserved for more aerodynamic models like the Lucid Air — or smaller, lighter crossovers like the Subaru Solterra and Toyota bZ. Seeing a boxy SUV deliver this kind of real-world mileage proves how much Hyundai has refined the Ioniq 5's powertrain efficiency.

Despite its compact crossover footprint, the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5 feels remarkably open and spacious on the inside thanks to its flat floor and long wheelbase. Both front and rear riders get generous legroom, with back-seat passengers easily stretching out thanks to 39.4 inches of space.

Recent findings suggest that I’m also a fan of Hyundai’s H-Tex seating upholstery, mainly due to how it strikes a great balance between plush cushioning and everyday durability — the seats feel soft and supportive right away, yet the material comes across as rugged enough to handle accidental spills. Around back, that spacious theme carries over into an expansive trunk with a wide opening and plenty of room for luggage, groceries, or bulky gear, offering 26.3 cubic feet of accessible cargo space.

In a recent development, yes, the design of the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5 hasn’t changed much from previous years, but I can’t help falling in love all over again with the headlights. Hyundai’s signature Parametric Pixel design language remains one of its biggest visual cues, anchored up front by its distinctive stacked LED headlights.

Recent findings suggest that unlike conventional round headlights, the slit-like light bars around the hood and squared-off pixel clusters give the front fascia a charming, retro-futuristic edge that still turns heads. Beyond looking great, the crisp LED projector beams cast a bright light pattern on dark roads.

It has been revealed that for a crossover with generous interior space, the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5 XRT feels surprisingly agile. Thanks to its low-mounted battery pack and dual-motor HTRAC AWD setup, it delivers instant acceleration off the line and stays remarkably planted through tighter corners and highway lane changes.

The steering is well-weighted without feeling heavy, and I personally prefer setting Hyundai’s regenerative braking paddles to their most aggressive level, which likely contributes to its superb efficiency.

Hyundai continues to set the bar for camera visibility in mainstream EVs thanks to how generous it is with premium features. While most EVs come with backup cameras at the very least, the 2026 Ioniq 5 is equipped with a Blind-Spot View Monitor that pops the camera feed directly into the 12.3-inch digital instrument cluster, giving me an unobstructed look at adjacent lanes before I merge.

Sources indicate that that thoughtfulness carries over to the 360-degree Surround View Monitor, which stitches together a sharp overhead view of the vehicle on the center display. Combined with multiple angled curb views and parking distance sensors, maneuvering the Ioniq 5 into tight parking spots is a breeze.

In a recent development, I’ve been in so many different vehicles this year that there are probably fewer than a dozen that stand out for their interior aesthetics. Unfortunately, the Ioniq 5 won’t make the cut this time around. While the exterior still turns heads, the cabin is starting to show its age and feels overdue for a proper refresh.

The dual 12.3-inch display setup and physical climate controls remain intuitive, but the minimalist gray-heavy trim comes off as boring by today's standards. Put it up against newer rivals like the 2027 Rivian R2 — with its warmer materials, cleaner architectural lines, and far more modern cabin styling — and the Ioniq 5's interior starts to look noticeably bland.

Sources indicate that as much impressed as I am by the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5’s efficiency and sub-$50K as-tested cost, there are quite simply more compelling options out there. If you're willing to stretch your budget just a bit higher, the 2027 Rivian R2 Performance immediately stands out with fresher styling, a far cooler and more modern interior, a spacious frunk, and drop-down rear glass.

On the flip side, if you want to save money without giving up capability, the 2026 Subaru Trailseeker undercuts the Ioniq 5 on price — while offering way more cargo room, higher towing and roof-rack utility, and the kind of brand recognition that makes it an easier everyday sell.

It has been revealed that even with tougher competition, the 2026 Hyundai Ioniq 5 is still well worth buying. Sure, its cabin is starting to look a bit dated, but its standout 3.9 mi/kWh efficiency, generous rear legroom, and sharp camera tech continue to make it one of the most well-rounded electric crossovers on the road.

In fact, it remains the EV I’m most inclined to recommend in Hyundai’s entire lineup, striking a sweet spot that neither the smaller Kona Electric nor the pricier three-row Ioniq 9 quite matches for everyday versatility.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the Diplomat is a show that loves mess (complimentary).
  • In a recent development, if you’ve been following the Wylers’ emotional journey up the power ladder as Kate navigates her role as the U.S.
  • Released in 2009, In the Loop doesn’t have the modern edge of The Diplomat, but it perfectly captures a similar sense that international diplomacy is being conducted by people with an affinity for chaos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the Diplomat is a show that loves mess (complimentary). Kate Wyler (Keri Russel) is a mess in many ways, and almost every major character is at emotional, moral, or intellectual loose ends. This would all be in good fun if these characters weren’t also some of the most powerful people in the world—presidents, prime ministers, and the high-level politicians and diplomats that serve them.

In a recent development, if you’ve been following the Wylers’ emotional journey up the power ladder as Kate navigates her role as the U.S. ambassador to the United Kingdom during what could be described as tumultuous times (and you’ve watched all our series streamalikes), allow me to suggest the one perfect movie that delivers similar vibes: 2009's In the Loop.

Released in 2009, In the Loop doesn’t have the modern edge of The Diplomat, but it perfectly captures a similar sense that international diplomacy is being conducted by people with an affinity for chaos. It’s actually a spinoff from a British TV series from the same co-writer/director, Armando Iannucci: The Thick of It. Many of the characters and situations are based on some of the people actually running the U.K., but you don’t need to be familiar with the show or the real history to enjoy the heck out of this movie. That goes double for Peter Capaldi’s absolutely ferocious performance as Malcolm Tucker, a man so creative with his profanity that many of his F-bombs will live rent-free in your head for years to come.

When a not-so-bright minister in the U.K. government (played by Tom Hollander) makes some dimwitted remarks that threaten to blow up Britain's carefully crafted diplomatic messaging around potential military adventures in the Middle East, Tucker (the prime minister's director of communications) has to tamp down the growing chaos that results. This eventually requires a contingent of British diplomats and officials to head to Washington, where they are quickly overwhelmed by the superpower vibes they encounter.

According to recent reports, it’s a more profane, faster-paced, and outright comedic story than The Diplomat, but it’s also easy to imagine most of the characters showing up on that show. The film also shares that same sense of controlled chaos that drives The Diplomat—the idea that a handful of tired, dedicated people are continuously racing around to prevent World War III even as dumber and more powerful people keep creating newly introduced crises. If Kate Wyler’s constant state of exhausted anxiety is your jam, you’ll love this movie. Stream In the Loop on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

In a recent development, want more cynical diplomats, secret aims, and international skulduggery with a side of personal emotional crises? Here are a few more movies fans of The Diplomat will love.

If you want a sense of what actual back-channel diplomacy is like, watch Ben Affleck’s Best Picture winner Argo, from 2012. Based on the remarkable true story of how six U.S. diplomats were rescued from Tehran during the Iran Hostage Crisis under cover of a fake sci-fi movie production, the film has the snappy energy and fast pace of The Diplomat combined with real-world danger. You can easily imagine Kate and Hal (Rufus Sewell) being part of the secret, off-the-books conversations that brought what’s known as the Canadian Caper into reality. Stream Argo on Paramount Plus or rent it on Prime Video.

If your favorite parts of The Diplomat are the schemes various players (mostly Kate and Hal) get up to in their efforts to shape world diplomacy and history to their liking, Wag the Dog is a good bet. When a sex scandal threatens to swing the Presidential election away from the incumbent, a spin doctor (Robert De Niro) wades in to save the day by convincing a top Hollywood producer (Dustin Hoffman) to “produce” a fake war in Albania to distract the American public. It’s equal parts funny, compelling, and depressingly instructive, and fans of the show will love the back-channel hijinks. Rent Wag the Dog on Prime Video.

One of the great things about The Diplomat is watching Kate Wyler, a smart and capable woman who generally knows more than anyone else in the room. If that’s the dynamic that grabs you, The Contender is the overlooked gem for you. When the vice president dies unexpectedly, the President (Jeff Bridges) nominates Senator Laine Hanson (Joan Allen) to take the post. A conservative senator (Gary Oldman) opposes her nomination and rolls out a smear campaign to derail her confirmation. There are dirty tricks and secret deals, and in the middle of it all, Allen’s terrific performance as a woman who refuses to back down in the face of sexist, unfair attacks. Stream The Contender on The Roku Channel, Kanopy, Hoopla, or Tubi, or rent it on Apple TV.

Nicole Kidman plays an interpreter at the United Nations, a woman who has a unique heritage and linguistic knowledge. When she overhears an assassination plot in an obscure dialect, she becomes embroiled in a dangerous game of espionage and high-stakes diplomacy as she races to prevent disaster (and keep herself alive). The Interpreter is a more serious and much more tense story, but it delves into the background work that makes the global system function, which puts it right in the sweet spot for fans of The Diplomat. Stream The Interpreter on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

Industry observers note that this might not seem like a match at first glance—a comedic treatment of the power struggle that followed the death of Soviet Premier Josef Stalin in 1953—but it absolutely is. Making a farce out of the political wrangling among the members of the Central Committee, the film has the same spirit as The Diplomat, showing that the people in charge are a bunch of schemers, tricksters, dummies, and sociopaths. Watching them run around making deals and angling for advantage offers the same energy as the show. Plus, it’s just plain hilarious. Stream The Death of Stalin on Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it's a big season for Abbott Elementary, as the ABC school-set sitcom celebrates a big milestone. The series will mark its 100th episode next month with a big trip to Disneyland, a theme park that just happens to be owned by ABC's corporate parent Disney. However, after airing its mid-season finale the next week, the show will go on hiatus over the holidays to return in the New Year.

In a recent development, much like the Super Bowl MVP, Abbott Elementary is going to Disneyland. The school's step team overcame the odds to win their regional finals, and the prize was an all-expenses-paid trip to the Anaheim theme park. Naturally, the school's teachers have been recruited as chaperones, and hijinks will ensue in the show's 100th episode, "One Hundred": it will premiere on December 2. A week later, on December 9, the show will air its winter finale, "Parents," which in which Jacob Hill (Chris Perfetti) will celebrate the holidays with a visit from his parents.

Don't worry: the show won't be gone for long. Abbott Elementary is set to return from its winter hiatus on January 13, 2027, with "Viral," an all-upcoming episode penned by Rebekka Pesqueira, a writer and story editor on the series. In fact, as that's the ninth episode of the season, it probably doesn't even stand as the midway mark, as Abbott's previous seasons (save for its first, when it was a mid-season replacement, and its third, which was interrupted by the Hollywood strikes) have all had 22 episodes.

Four love stories, four completely different ideas of what it means to be somebody's person. This is the one that matches how you actually fall, and what it would ask of you.

It has been revealed that you do not fall for strangers. You fall for the person you have already been talking to for years, which is the slowest and by some distance the most durable way anybody has found to do this.

You want a partner, not an audience. Somebody who wants their own life as badly as you want yours, and who would never ask you to be smaller to make the relationship easier.

The intensity was never the problem. The secrecy is. You are drawn to a love that lives entirely in private, and to the particular ache of wanting somebody you are not supposed to want.

Recent findings suggest that you do not do this cautiously. When it happens for you it is immediate and total and it rearranges everything, and you would not accept a smaller version of it.

There's been a bit of a shake-up at Abbott Elementary this season. After narrowly avoiding closure in the season 5 finale, Abbott has had to deal with an influx of new students from schools that weren't so lucky. That's strained their resources to the limits and necessitated bringing in a new assistant principal: Gregory Eddie (Tyler James Williams). It's appropriate, since he originally applied to be Abbott's principal, only to be relegated to supply teacher. He's also planning another big change: he's going to propose to girlfriend and fellow teacher Janine Teagues (Quinta Brunson). Meanwhile, Principal Ava Coleman (Janelle James) is still adjusting to being in a relationship with the working-class O'Shon (Matthew Law), Jacob and Melissa Schemmenti (Lisa Ann Walter) are still at-times uneasy housemates, and Barbara Howard (Sheryl Lee Ralph) is contemplating retirement. Janitor Mr. Johnson (William Stanford Davis) continues to be Mr. Johnson.

Abbott Elementary will return to ABC on January 13, 2027, with "Viral." Stay tuned to Collider for future updates.

Latest Update: ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ Review: ‘Friday Night Lights’ Meets ‘Five Came Back’ in Peter Berg’s Formulaic Netflix Movie About a World War II Football Game
